## Need to know

### What to bring

*   Wear sturdy walking shoes suitable for uphill terrain and unpaved paths.

*   Don’t forget a hat, sunscreen, and water to stay comfortable throughout your visit.

*   Please carry your own earphones for the best audio experience.

### What’s not allowed

*   Food and drink are restricted in some areas, especially within the Castle.

*   Alcohol is not permitted within the site.

*   Due to venue restrictions, pets cannot tag along for this experience

### Accessibility

*   The castle grounds include uneven paths and steep climbs, which may not be suitable for individuals with mobility challenges.

*   There is limited wheelchair access.

### Additional Information

*   Entry Tickets and Entry Tickets + Audio Guide options are valid for 90 days from the date of purchase.

*   Audio guide is available on the Headout app. Instructions to download will be shared with your ticket. Do bring your own headphones.

*   Ticket holders can visit anytime during opening hours.

*   Expect crowds during peak times; early visits are recommended for a quieter experience.

*   After booking, you will receive an email with further instructions on how to access and download your audio tour. Please check your email spam folder as well.

*   The castle is closed on January 1, May 1, Dec 24 and 25.

*   Please check your final voucher for the starting point details & specific instructions.

# Lisbon Cathedral

Lisbon Cathedral, better known as **Sé de Lisboa**, is the oldest and most important church in the city.Its construction dates back to the **12th century** and is predominantly **Romanesque** in style.

![Image 4: Lisbon Cathedral, Maria Maior de Lisboa](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/catedral-lisboa.jpg)

**The Cathedral of Lisbon** is austere in appearance with a predominantly **Romanesque style**, although with the alterations made over the years, different styles have been masterfully blended, which give it a very special character.

From the outside, the cathedral is protected by **thick walls framed** by two bell towers, which give it an appearance more typical of **a medieval fortress than of a church**. The façade still retains its **12th-century Romanesque style** and its centerpiece is a central rose window.

Once inside, we'll find a temple that, amid its **austere character**, has some decorative elements such as the fountain in which Saint Anthony of Padua was baptized,some 14th-century sarcophagi, and a striking 14th-century Gothic chapel.

## Looking at the Past

Throughout its **[history](https://www.lisbon.net/history)**, the Lisbon Cathedral has become one of the most important examples of Portuguese fortification, surviving in an exemplary manner and standing tall after being hit with different **natural disasters**,after which it had to be **renovated on several occasions**.

The Lisbon Cathedral experienced its **worst catastrophe during the Great Earthquake of 1755**. On November 1 of this year, the city was shaken to its core in a tragic episode that would destroy much of the city, severely attacking the temple, after which the cathedral underwent a major renovation.

## History of São Jorge Castle

The history of São Jorge Castle dates back to the 11th century when the Moors built it during their occupation of the Iberian Peninsula. It was initially called the Castle of Alcáçova and was used as a fortress to defend Lisbon from invading forces. In 1147, the castle was captured by Christian forces led by King Afonso Henriques in the Siege of Lisbon, and it became a royal palace and residence of the Portuguese monarchy.

Over the centuries, the castle underwent several renovations and expansions, adding various architectural styles to its design, such as Gothic and Manueline. In the 16th century, the castle served as a military stronghold during the Spanish occupation of Portugal.

During the 20th century, the castle was restored and opened to the public as a historical landmark and a tourist attraction. Today, it serves as a cultural center, hosting exhibitions and events that showcase Portugal's rich history and culture.

## Who built São Jorge Castle?

The construction of São Jorge Castle is attributed to the Moors who occupied the Iberian Peninsula in the 11th century. The castle was initially built as a military fortress to defend Lisbon from invading forces. The original design of the castle reflects the Moorish architectural style, characterized by the use of limestone and granite, as well as the incorporation of horseshoe arches, decorative tiles, and geometric patterns. Throughout the centuries, the castle underwent several renovations and expansions, adding various architectural styles to its design, such as Gothic and Manueline.

The construction of the castle did not involve any specific architect as it was built by the Moors as a military stronghold. However, its architectural significance lies in its blend of different styles, reflecting the various periods of its history. The castle remains a testimony to the diverse cultural heritage of Lisbon and Portugal, attracting visitors from all over the world who come to admire its architecture and learn about its rich history.

# Belém

Picturesque Belém is home to some of **Lisbon's most important monuments**, such as the Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Tower, absolutely unmissable!

[Reserve Your Tour](https://www.civitatis.com/en/lisbon/lisbon-belem-tour/?aid=804&guide_id=45 "Reserve Your Tour")

![Image 4: Jerónimos Monastery](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/jeronimos-belem.jpg)

Jerónimos Monastery Monument to the Discoveries

![Image 5: Paséis de Belém](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/belem-pasteleria.jpg)

The famous Portuguese pastries

2 See photo gallery

Belém is the southwesternmost district of Lisbon. Far from the city center, but easily accessible, this neighborhood is located at the mouth of the River Tagus. **Portugal’s various explorers set sail from this part of town** to other parts of the world and brought back riches and their many discoveries.

## What to See in Belém

Belém houses **two incredibly famous landmarks**. The first is **[Jerónimos Monastery](https://www.lisbon.net/jeronimos-monastery "Jéronimos Monastery ")** (Mosteiro dos Jerónimos) and the second is **[Belém Tower](https://www.lisbon.net/belem-tower "Belém Tower")** (Torre de Belém). In addition, travelers will also enjoy exploring the [Monument to the Discoveries](https://www.lisbon.net/monument-discoveries) (Padrão dos Descobrimentos), the **[25 de Abril Bridge](https://www.lisbon.net/25th-april-bridge)**, and the **[National Coach Museum](https://www.lisbon.net/national-coach-museum)**.

Another must when visiting Belém is to stop at Pastéis de Belém, which used to be a small shop attached to a sugar cane refinery, to **try its pastéis de Belém**, a typical and delicious Portuguese egg tart pastry or custard tarts invented in this small shop in 1837.

*   **[Tour of Belém + Palace of Ajuda Tour](https://www.civitatis.com/en/lisbon/belem-palace-ajuda-tour?aid=804&guide_id=45 "Tour por Belém y el Palacio de Ajuda")**

## Getting to Belém

The easiest way to get to Belém from Lisbon’s city center is to take the **[tram nº 15](https://www.lisbon.net/tram "Trams in Lisbon")** at the Cais do Sodré station, in the **[Praça do Comércio](https://www.lisbon.net/commerce-square)**. It's usually packed with people traveling to Belém.

When you get on the tram, **be careful of pickpockets**. This is a very popular line for professional thieves since it's always full of tourists.

# Lisbon's Neighborhoods

**Lisbon is divided into several clearly distinguishable neighbourhoods.** To really get to know Portugal’s capital, you’ll need to spend time exploring each one of these districts.

The most traditional neighborhoods are [Baixa](https://www.lisbon.net/baixa),[Chiado](https://www.lisbon.net/chiado-bairro-alto),[Bairro Alto](https://www.lisbon.net/chiado-bairro-alto), **[Alfama](https://www.lisbon.net/alfama)**,and **[Belém](https://www.lisbon.net/belem)**. Each one of these districts has its own unique vitality and essence.

In addition to these traditional areas, there are two very modern areas of Lisbon. The first is called **[Marquess of Pombal Square](https://www.lisbon.net/marquess-pombal-square)****(Praça do Marquês de Pombal)**and its surroundings. The second is the area around the **[Park of the Nations](https://www.lisbon.net/park-of-the-nations) (Parque das Nações),** which was built for the 1998 Lisbon World Exposition.

## Neighbourhoods

[![Image 3: Baixa](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/guia/baixa-grid.jpg)](https://www.lisbon.net/baixa "Baixa")

### [Baixa](https://www.lisbon.net/baixa "Baixa")

 Baixa is the liveliest and most central neighborhood in Lisbon. It was rebuilt by the Marquis of Pombal after the Great Earthquake of 1755. 

[![Image 4: Chaido & Bairro Alto](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/guia/chiado-barrio-alto-grid.jpg)](https://www.lisbon.net/chiado-bairro-alto "Chaido & Bairro Alto")

### [Chaido & Bairro Alto](https://www.lisbon.net/chiado-bairro-alto "Chaido & Bairro Alto")

 Chiado and Bairro Alto are Lisbon’s bohemian and alternative neighborhoods. They are separated by the square Praça Luís de Camões. 

[![Image 5: Alfama](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/guia/alfama-grid.jpg)](https://www.lisbon.net/alfama "Alfama")

### [Alfama](https://www.lisbon.net/alfama "Alfama")

 Alfama is an authentic fishing neighborhood located between the Altantic Ocean and Lisbon’s São Jorge Castle. It is where Fado was created. 

[![Image 6: Belém](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/guia/belem-grid.jpg)](https://www.lisbon.net/belem "Belém")

### [Belém](https://www.lisbon.net/belem "Belém")

 Lisbon’s neighborhood Belém houses two beautiful points of interest, the Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower. You can also try delicious pastéis de Belém.

# Jerónimos Monastery

The Jerónimo Monastery is, along with the Belém Tower, the most important tourist attraction in Lisbon,**inside which lies the tomb of Vasco de Gama.**

![Image 4: Jerónimos Monastery](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/monasterio-jeronimos.jpg)

Jerónimos Monastery

![Image 5: Church of Santa Maria](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/iglesia-jeronimos.jpg)

Church of Santa Maria

![Image 6: Jerónimos Monastery, cloister](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/claustro-jeronimos.jpg)

Cloister of the Jerónimos Monastery

3 See photo gallery

The **Jerónimos Monastery** (also known as the Hieronymites Monastery)is, along with the Tower of Belém, one of the most visited sites in Lisbon. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, this landmark was designed by the Portuguese architect**Diogo de Boitaca,**to serve as a final resting-place for members of the House of Avizto. It also serves as a resting place for other legendary Portuguese figures, including explorer**Vasco da Gama**, the first European to reach India by sea.

The construction began on 6 January 1501 and wasn’t completed until **the seventeenth century.**The building is predominantly Manueline style (Portuguese late Gothic). Curiously, the monastery was built on the site of the former **Ermida do Restelo,** the chapel where Vasco da Gama and the rest of the sailors prayed before setting sail down the African coast to India.

## Buy Tickets to Jerónimos Monastery

There are a number of different ways of visiting the Jerónimos Monastery:

### Jerónimos Monastery Official Tickets

Visit the monastery and explore it at your own speed by buying an[**official ticket to the Jerónimos Monastery with Civitatis**](https://www.civitatis.com/en/lisbon/jeronimos-monastery-tickets?aid=804&guide_id=45 "Jerónimos Monastery Ticket").

### Lisboa Card (Lisbon Tourist Card)

If you're looking to make the most of your trip to Lisbon at the best price, the Lisboa Card (Lisbon Card) includes access to 50+ attractions and free travel on public transport.

# São Jorge Castle history: timeline, key events, evolution

1.   [Castelo De São Jorge Tickets](https://www.saojorgecastletickets.com/)
2.   History

​[São Jorge Castle](https://www.saojorgecastletickets.com/) is a medieval castle dating back to the 9th century. Perched atop the highest hill overlooking the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, the historic castle houses a museum and the remains of a royal palace. The castle is a National Monument and is a treat for history and archaeology buffs.

## São Jorge Castle timeline

*   **10th century:** Islamic ruler Hisham II ordered large-scale construction on the site.  
*   **1147**: Dom Afonso Henriques, the first King of Portugal, captured Lisbon from the Moors.  
*   **1580**: The castle was converted into a military base. Later, it was transformed into a prison and hospital.  
*   **1755**: A severe earthquake hit the castle and the palace.  
*   **1910**: São Jorge Castle was declared a National Monument by an official decree.

## History of São Jorge Castle explained

![Image 2: Aerial view of Sao Jorge Castle in Lisbon with surrounding cityscape.](https://cdn-imgix.headout.com/media/images/4765c407c2b406e56c10d758d134a1b9-saojorgecastle.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&crop=faces&fit=crop&w=3840&q=50)

1/3

### Iron Age population

The hill in Santa Maria Maior where Sao Jorge Castle is located has been a place of interest for various civilizations since the Iron Age. Some archaeological studies suggest that the area was first occupied by Celts. It was also home to Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans. A strategic location, close to the port, Lisbon was crucial to the Roman Empire. In 48 BC, the Romans created the first fortification on the hilltop. The construction of large buildings and the wall commenced only during the time of the Moors, in the 9th and 10th centuries. Interestingly, there is no consensus among historians as to whether the Moors built the castle that stands today.

### Moors

The earliest trace of Islamic settlement on the hill dates back to the 8th century in the Umayyad caliphate period. Some inscriptions show that it was the Islamic ruler Hisam II who ordered the construction of the walls and buildings. The construction was supervised by the statesman Almanzor. The archaeological evidence pointing to the fortification dates back to 985. It describes Lisbon as a Madina, the traditional walled city in the Islamic world. Historians believe the reference shows that Lisbon was a walled city during the period of the Moors, and construction was prevalent.

### The Reconquest

The political tug of war between invading Moors and Christian rulers intensified in the 12th century. In 1147, Afonso Henriques, the first King of Portugal, reclaimed the city of Lisbon in the crusade. The military campaign known as the reconquest effectively ended the rule of Moors in Europe. As a result, Sao Jorge Castle became one of the prized possessions of the campaign. After the reconquest, the castle underwent several modifications. Historians are not sure about the changes made to the castle immediately after the crusade, but inscriptions refer to the castle during the time of King D. Afonso III and his son, D. Dinis. In the 13th century, the castle also served as a residential area, and later in the 14th century, as a hospital.

## Construction of São Jorge Castle

The only piece of authoritative evidence suggesting construction atop the hill is an inscription dated to 985. It was during the reign of the Moors, in the Umayyad caliphate. The information describes Lisbon as Madina, meaning it was a walled city. It also mentions that the wall is damaged and needs repair. Despite it being widely accepted that a fortified citadel existed within the walls, historians are silent on whether it was Sao Jorge Castle. The primary reason for this is that Sao Jorge Castle is a Gothic castle with a distinctive quadrangular layout and towers. It was heavily modified after the Christian reconquest of Lisbon, and at least eight Christian rulers oversaw extensive modifications to the fort. A massive earthquake in 1755 also affected the castle and its buildings, altering some of its characteristics.

​[São Jorge Castle Facts](https://www.saojorgecastletickets.com/facts/)

## São Jorge Castle today

![Image 3: Aerial view of Sao Jorge Castle in Lisbon, Portugal, with cityscape in the background.](https://cdn-imgix.headout.com/media/images/95843abd87897a3652b138db5662eda6-AerialviewofSaoJorgecastleorSt.GeorgecastleatLisboncity-Portugal.jpg?auto=compress%2Cformat&w=1222.3999999999999&h=687.6&q=90&ar=16%3A9&crop=faces&fit=crop)

Today, São Jorge Castle stands as a proud symbol of Portugal's eventful history. The imposing castle, overlooking Lisbon, is a treat for enthusiasts of archaeology and history. It houses several attractions, with the museum being the most important among them all. It exhibits invaluable historical treasures. The partially ruined Royal Palace is also a must-visit. The architecture of the rooms is marvelous. There are two public squares giving unmatched views of the city of Lisbon and the river Tagus. Scattered around the fort are fourteen pieces of original artillery. There are statues of rulers and extensively landscaped gardens in which the majestic Indian peacocks stroll.

## Frequently asked questions about São Jorge Castle

### What is the historical significance of São Jorge Castle?

Sao Jorge Castle Castle is synonymous with history. It was constructed during the 9th and 10th centuries. First occupied by the Moors and later by Christians through a historic battle, Sao Jorge Castle tells the story of medieval Europe's eventful past.

### How old is São Jorge Castle?

Although historians differ on the exact date of the construction of the structure, it is estimated to have been completed in the 10th century.

### How many years did it take to build São Jorge Castle?

Sao Jorge, or at least its fortifications, was built during the 9th and 10th centuries. After the reconquest in 1147, several modifications were made to Sao Jorge.

### Who built São Jorge Castle?

Some inscriptions credit the Moor ruler Hisam II as the man behind the construction of the citadel. More accurate archaeological evidence suggests Portugal's first King, Afonso Henriques, was responsible for the modifications.

### What is the architectural style of Sao Jorge castle?

Sao Jorge follows the traditional Gothic style. It has a quadrangular layout, an elbow-shaped gateway, and 10 quadrangular turrets. To strengthen defense, a barbican was built in the southeastern area.

### What events or incidents have shaped the history of São Jorge Castle?

The reconquest in 1147 was the most eventful among all instances, as it reshaped its history. The earthquake in 1755 also played an important role as it damaged some buildings, changing the utility of the structure.

### What are some lesser-known historical facts or anecdotes about São Jorge Castle?

There was a palace inside the Sao Jorge citadel, which was eventually lost to the earthquake. Also, in the later part of history, the castle served as a prison and hospital for soldiers

# Igreja de Santa Cruz do Castelo - Church

[Play Audio](javascript:void(0))|[Show Directions](javascript:void(0)) 

    *   ![Image 26: Igreja de Santa Cruz do Castelo - Church on Lisbon audio tour Castelo de São Jorge and Bairro do Castelo: A Lisbon Walking Tour](https://media.voicemap.me/uploads/sound_bite_image/image/40281/webp_full/20201215_165855.webp)

As you get to the crossroads ahead, turn right.

You will then enter a small square called Largo de Santa Cruz do Castelo.

When you’re there, go to the left, towards the big white building and stop once you reach it.

(6 seconds silence)

This is the Igreja de Santa Cruz do Castelo, or Church of the Holy Cross of the Castle. Having been built upon an ancient mosque right after the conquest of Lisbon in 1147, this was Lisbon’s first Christian temple.

Throughout the centuries, this church was damaged by several earthquakes, before being totally destroyed by the big seism of 1755. It was therefore rebuilt to its actual shape during the second half of the 18th century.

The shortage of construction materials and the vast number of buildings which were in need of a hasty repair or reconstruction after that catastrophic event explain the very sober, plain style applied to this church.

Now please walk along the side of the Church towards its back end.

(2 seconds silence)

Can you see the small door in front of you?

(1 second silence)

This is the entrance to the Church’s Tower, which is worth a short visit.

Having been built over a defensive tower which was part of the original Moorish wall, it used to be part of the Palace of the Alcáçova.

It was also reconstructed to its actual shape in the late 18th century.

Once you get to the top, you will not only be rewarded with one of the best views over the East part of Lisbon, but also you we be able to toll one of the Tower’s four big bronze bells.   
  
(4 seconds silence)

After you’ve finished exploring the Tower of the Church of Santa Cruz do Castelo, please head down the stairs and return to the square.

When you’re there, go across the courtyard, in direction of the narrow street next to the dark pink house with the coat of arms showing a lion standing above its main door.

# Tour Start - Rua do Chão da Feira

[Play Audio](javascript:void(0))|[Show Directions](javascript:void(0)) 

    *   ![Image 26: Tour Start - Rua do Chão da Feira on Lisbon audio tour Castelo de São Jorge and Bairro do Castelo: A Lisbon Walking Tour](https://media.voicemap.me/uploads/sound_bite_image/image/40251/webp_full/20220722_112042.webp)

Hello, and welcome to the Castle of São Jorge.

Thank you for choosing this Self-Guided Immersive Audio Tour, proposed by Eo - Immersive Audio Tours™.

My name is Marco, and I’ll be your host for the next 75 minutes.

I’ve always been passionate about history and I’m eager to share some untold stories about the Castle of Lisbon and its surrounding neighborhood that have been forgotten in the sands of time.

If you’re standing next to the Castle’s outer walls, near the arched gateway, you’re in the right place to start this Tour.

The Castle of São Jorge is one of the most iconic symbols of Lisbon. Its massive yellow stone walls, which majestically dominate the whole historical center and the access to the Tagus river, can be seen from every part of the city.

Standing proudly from one of Lisbon’s highest hills, peaking at 110 meters, this is the most visited historical site in Portugal, with nearly two million visitors every year.

Before we start our visit to the Castle of São Jorge and its surroundings, let me explain how VoiceMap works.

The app uses your GPS location to play audio automatically, at the right time and place. This means that you can put your phone away now. Don’t worry if I’m silent for a while, when I’m not giving directions or telling stories. There’s a map on your screen if you ever feel lost, and if you do get way off track without noticing, VoiceMap will let you know.

So, let’s start walking.

With your back to the Castle’s wall, please move towards the big rounded arch gateway to the right, which grants access to the fortress’ inner boundaries.

(4 seconds silence)

Let’s stop here for a moment.

(1 second silence)

In spite of its ancient looks, this arch was only built in the mid-19th century.

It is a fine example of the architectural style inspired by Romanticism, which placed its emphasis on emotion, and the glorification of all the past and nature, focusing particularly on the medieval period.

On top of the gateway, in the middle, you will find the ancient coat of arms of the Kingdom of Portugal, with the date 4-4-1846 written below it.

Now go across the arch and keep going until you hear me again.

(5 seconds silence)

To the left you will see a small colorful statue of Saint George standing in a stone recess, protected by a glass window.   
This famous saint became the patron of Portugal and its Army in the 14th century. It is since also the protector of the Castle of Lisbon, to which it gave its name.

Keep going up the street.

## Highlights

*   Grab these tickets and head to Lisbon's most famous landmark, São Jorge Castle, an 11th-century gem that dominates the Lisbon skyline.

*   Explore the expertly curated Permanent Exhibitions section to learn all about its past life as a military base and the siege of 1147.

*   See beautiful art like the sculpture of Afonso I, the first king of Portugal, and discover elements of early Islamic architecture.

*   Upgrade to include a multilingual audio guide or local guide for rich historical commentary and fun local legends, or choose a tour of the castle with a walking tour of Alfama.

## Need to know

### What to bring

*   Wear sturdy walking shoes suitable for uphill terrain and unpaved paths.

*   Don’t forget a hat, sunscreen, and water to stay comfortable throughout your visit.

*   Please carry your own earphones for the best audio experience.

### What’s not allowed

*   Food and drink are restricted in some areas, especially within the Castle.

*   Alcohol is not permitted within the site.

*   Due to venue restrictions, pets cannot tag along for this experience

### Accessibility

*   The castle grounds include uneven paths and steep climbs, which may not be suitable for individuals with mobility challenges.

*   There is limited wheelchair access.

### Additional Information

*   Entry Tickets and Entry Tickets + Audio Guide options are valid for 90 days from the date of purchase.

*   Audio guide is available on the Headout app. Instructions to download will be shared with your ticket. Do bring your own headphones.

*   Ticket holders can visit anytime during opening hours.

*   Expect crowds during peak times; early visits are recommended for a quieter experience.

*   After booking, you will receive an email with further instructions on how to access and download your audio tour. Please check your email spam folder as well.

*   The castle is closed on January 1, May 1, Dec 24 and 25.

# Alfama

Alfama is one of Lisbon's most traditional neighborhoods, whose narrow streets were **home to fishermen**back in the day.

[Book a Free Tour](https://www.civitatis.com/en/lisbon/free-tour-alfama/?aid=804&guide_id=45 "Book a Free Tour")

![Image 4: Alfama](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/alfama.jpg)

A street in Alfama district

![Image 5: Museu do Fado](https://www.civitatis.com/f/portugal/lisboa/galeria/thumbs/museo-do-fado.jpg)

Museu do Fado

2 See photo gallery

**Alfama is an old, gentle and humble fishing suburb in Lisbon.** Located at the foot of São Jorge Castle, between the hill and the ocean, this neighbourhood holds the essence of the city. It's an area full of aromas and mixed emotions, and it's where [Fado](https://www.lisbon.net/fado "Fado in Lisbon")was created back in the 1820s. If you're not familiar with Fado,it’s the best-known genre of Portuguese music, very melancholic and often about the sea.

The area where Alfama currently sits was already**inhabited during the Visigoth period**. The Romans also left their stamp with the ruins of a Roman Theatre, built under Augustus during 1 century BC. It's located inside the Cathedral on the Rua da Saudade. Sadly, **most of the Christian churches were destroyed in the earthquake of 1755.**

If you visit the top part of Alfama (near the São Jorge Castle), you’ll get some impressive views of the whole neighbourhood which runs down to the Tagus River and of its port.

If you want to learn more about Fado music, the **Fado Museum is in this part of town.**

## Getting to Alfama

Alfama’s steep and narrow hills, which have inspired numerous Fado verses, are too restricted for four-wheeled vehicles.

To get to the top part of this unique suburb, you can either walk from the centre or take **the nostalgic**[nº 28 tram](https://www.lisbon.net/tram "Nostalgic tram 28 "), which we highly recommend, as it’s a charming and comfortable way of travelling through Alfama. It leaves you at the highest point of Alfama.

# São Jorge Castle Tickets

Climb the ramparts of Lisbon’s legendary hilltop fortress.

Great for couples Hidden gem Historic landmark

### Castelo de São Jorge Tickets

[**🏛️ São Jorge Castle: Fast Track Ticket + Guided Tour**](link_10)

1-hour expert-led tour with fast track access. Includes live guide in English, French, Portuguese, or Spanish, groups of up to 30 people, and deep historical insights about Moorish origins and royal history.

[**🏷️ Lisboa Card: 51 Attractions + Transport**](link_11)

Includes free São Jorge Castle entry plus 50 other attractions and unlimited public transport. Available for 24h (€31), 48h (€51), or 72h (€62). Best value for multi-attraction visits.

## Benefits

*   Take in a unique view of the city with the Camera Obscura in the Ulysses Tower.
*   Skip the queues at the ticket office and head straight to the entrance when you buy your ticket online.
*   Spot the peacocks showing off their feathers.

## Tickets & Prices

The castle offers [general admission tickets](link_12) that include full access to the fortress, archaeological site, gardens, and all exhibitions. Your ticket also includes guided tours of the castle (“Discovering the Castle”) and the Camera Obscura experience in the Tower of Ulysses.

Tickets are available for adults aged 18 to 64, with discounted rates available for seniors aged 65+, individuals with disabilities, and those aged 6 to 17 (just make sure to bring a valid ID). Children under 6 get in for free.

You should buy tickets online to skip the ticket queues when you arrive. Book online through authorized resellers like [Tiqets](link_13), which often come with better refundable policies and allow you to secure timed entry for your preferred date.

[Check ticket availability and latest prices »](link_14)

### Lisboa Card

**Get FREE admission to Castelo de São Jorge**plus 50+ other top Lisbon attractions! Includes unlimited public transport and discounts at restaurants and shops.

[Check Availability](link_15)

## Plan Your Visit

Prepare to explore Saint George’s Castle with all the essential information you need for an effortless visit.

### Opening Hours

| Months | Opening Hours | Last Entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open Daily, Winter (November to February) | 9:00 – 18:00 | 17:30 |
| Open Daily, Summer (March to October) | 9:00 – 21:00 | 20:30 |

Closed: January 1st, May 1st, December 24th, 25th, and 31st.

#### Best Times to Visit

Visit in autumn (September to October) or spring (April to June) to wander the grounds in temperate weather without the typical summertime bustle of July and August.

Ditch the crowds and arrive about 20 minutes before they open or around 15:30 when the grounds are less busy.

### How to Get There

Whether you prefer a quick and direct route or a scenic journey through the city’s cobblestoned streets, there’s a perfect way for you to get to Castelo de São Jorge.

#### Tram

Head down to Praça Martim Moniz for a five-minute ride on tram 28 through iconic neighbourhoods like Graça before getting off at the Largo das Portas do Sol stop in Alfama. Keep in mind that this tram is really popular among tourists, so you might have to queue.

Or, use tram 12 for a 10-minute trip through the more off-the-tourist-map areas like Rua dos Lagares before getting off at Largo das Portas do Sol stop. From there, head uphill along Rua de Santa Cruz do Castelo, where the castle is around a 5-minute walk away.

#### Bus

Want to skip the uphill walk? Catch bus 737 from Praça da Figueira for a quick ride straight to the castle. It’s not a very scenic route, but it gets you right to the top, just a short walk from the entrance, in eight minutes.

#### Metro

Start by taking the Green Line metro to Martim Moniz station, where you can then board tram 12 or 28 and disembark at Largo das Portas do Sol. Alternatively, take the metro to Rossio station and exit towards Praça da Figueira.

From there, you can either walk a fairly steep 15 minutes to the castle, following Rua Condes de Monsanto and using the lift in Chão do Loureiro’s parking lot, or just catch bus 737 if you prefer to skip the climb.

#### Car

Lisbon’s historic areas aren’t ideal for driving, with narrow, winding streets and limited parking. The closest car parks to Castelo de São Jorge are at Chão do Loureiro and Portas do Sol, around 5-10 minutes from the castle on foot.

If you’re driving and have specific accessibility needs, contact EMEL (a municipal company in Lisbon) a day in advance to receive an access code for the castle’s private parking area. Then contact the ticket office for clearance.

### Map & Address

#### Castelo de Sao Jorge

![Image 2: Map of Castelo de Sao Jorge](blob:http://localhost/ed27c64051af73802bcef4e3adf802b5 [link_16])

R. de Santa Cruz do Castelo, 1100-129 Lisboa, Portugal · [Google Maps](https://maps.google.com/?q=38.7139092,-9.1334762)

### Accessibility

This castle’s medieval architecture means some areas aren’t wheelchair-friendly, including the tower, battlements, and walkways. However, the site has added features to help improve accessibility, like the option to book an inclusive visit in advance.

Ramps are at the ticket office and museum entrance, with a lift inside to access the Islamic period room. There’s an accessible route to the eastern viewpoint, a wheelchair-friendly bathroom, four wheelchairs, and one Swiss-Trac wheelchair available upon request.

## What to See & Do (with Pictures)

From finding the castle’s peacocks wandering the grounds of history dating back as far as the Iron Age to hilltop scenery that demands photos, São Jorge Castle is a treat for view-chasers and those who like to feel the past under their feet.

### The Battlements and Towers

![Image 3: Visitors walking along the battlements of Castelo de São Jorge with towers, trees, and river views in the background.](blob:http://localhost/ccb92d2224062138d874851e6f1c6460 [link_17])artfotoss/[Depositphotos](link_18)

It’s safe to say that the imposing towers on a military fort perched atop the highest hill in Lisbon (São Jorge Hill) made a powerful statement of dominance and protection. They also overlook the city and the Tagus River, which were intentional positions for observation and defense.

Battlements are stone walls with squared openings in them (crenels), which guards used to watch for enemies and shoot through while being protected by the parts without gaps (merlons). These battlements provide hands-on evidence of what it was like to guard Lisbon centuries ago.

### The Camera Obscura (Tower of Ulysses)

![Image 4: Ulysses Tower at Castelo de São Jorge in Lisbon.](blob:http://localhost/61e1b9ffdb7e5f1cf2a7e954f253bae4 [link_19])vkorost/[Depositphotos](link_20)

Once a royal archive named Torre do Tombo (Tower of the Archive), it’s now called the Tower of Ulysses, named after the Greek hero who, according to local legend, founded Lisbon. Today, the tower is home to the Camera Obscura, which is pretty much the early ancestor of a camera.

This ancient type of camera works by using a series of lenses and mirrors to project a live image of the outside onto a screen inside a darkened room. As the device moves, you get a surprisingly detailed image of the city in real-time, which is a fun way of seeing Lisbon in motion.

### Archaeological Site

![Image 5: Castelo de São Jorge seen from a distance above Lisbon rooftops with Portuguese and castle flags flying.](blob:http://localhost/7d85ed157cf9b246fb1b571a10edafe9 [link_21])vkorost/[Depositphotos](link_22)

The castle’s archaeological site reveals layers of Lisbon’s history and how it was shaped by the occupation of pre-Roman to Moorish civilisations before being conquered by the Kingdom of Portugal during the Siege of Lisbon in 1147.

Step back in time and check out the oldest preserved structures in the castle, which were potentially a kitchen and a fire area. Then have a look at some antique-as-it-gets pottery, including amphorae (traditional ancient Greek jugs with two handles).

### Gardens and Peacocks

![Image 6: People gathered at the scenic overlook in the gardens of Castelo de São Jorge with trees and a view of the 25 de Abril Bridge.](blob:http://localhost/1cdb69caf53963df457d75bc6f6b2c68 [link_23])pio3/[Depositphotos](link_24)

End your visit in the castle’s leafy escape, where you can relax and enjoy your surroundings under one of the many types of trees, including olive or cork oak. Head to the Place-of-Arms to see two of the castle’s most exotic tree species, the jacaranda and silk floss trees.

Keep an eye out for the resident Indian peacocks who strut around freely as if they know they steal the show. They’re loud and not shy about showing off their feathers — just don’t feed them your food. You can buy small packets of the appropriate food for them from the castle’s shop.

## Did You Know That? Facts

1.   Castelo de São Jorge endured major earthquakes in 1531 and 1755, with the second one having caused significant damage that is visible in the restoration “scars” today.
2.   The castle sees several bat species flying around the building after sunset — these unsung creatures play an essential role in pest and disease control.
3.   The Moniz Gate is named after Martim Moniz, a Portuguese knight who is said to have willingly sacrificed his life by using his body to keep the castle gates from being shut, allowing his comrades to enter and conquer it.
4.   Sundays in March to June and September to October are dedicated to family programmes.
5.   The castle is also a venue for events like weddings, corporate events, and private events.

## Insider Tips

1.   Prioritize comfort when you pick out your shoes, as this castle involves a lot of walking on uneven surfaces and steps.
2.   Stick around till sunset for some dreamy photos of the castle during golden hour.
3.   Take advantage of the castle’s epic vantage points by bringing binoculars or a camera with a zoom lens.
4.   Use the free dual-elevator system, Elevador do Castelo (Castle Elevator), located in Baixa, for an easy way up to the castle area.
5.   If you’re visiting with kids, be sure to keep your eyes peeled when you’re near the low walls and steep stairs.

## History

**7th-8th century**

The earliest evidence of human occupation is found.

**2nd century**

The Romans construct the first fortifications on the castle.

**10th century**

Islamic ruler Hisham II initiates large-scale construction on the site.

**11th century**

The Moors establish the castle as a defense structure.

**1147**

King Dom Afonso Henrique’s army conquers the castle from the Moors.

**1580**

The castle serves as a military base, hospital, and prison.

**1910**

Royal Decree declares the building a National Monument.

**1938**

Castelo de São Jorge is restored to the version we recognise today.

## FAQs

### What does the castle ticket include?

Full access to the monument and gardens, with an audio guide covering the castle’s history.

### Is São Jorge Castle free with the Lisboa Card?

Yes, entry is free with the [Lisboa Card](link_0).

### Do you need to buy tickets in advance?

Not required, but [booking online](link_25) or using your card lets you walk past the ticket line.

### How much time do I need to explore Castelo de São Jorge?

Around two hours for a top-to-bottom look.

### Is there free entry to the castle?

It’s a paid monument, though Lisbon residents qualify for free entry with proof of address.

# Castelo de São Jorge

Alfama, Lisbon, Portugal

![Image 1](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge1.jpg)![Image 2](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge5.jpg)![Image 3](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge2.jpg)![Image 4](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge4.jpg)![Image 5](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge3.jpg)

## why we love it

Set on the city's tallest hill (where its Middle-Age inhabitants could best see incoming threats), São Jorge Castle was originally built by the Moors, before it was captured by the Christians who eventually ruled the city. Despite its dramatic history, today, the castle is one of the city's most relaxing and tranquil places—there are peacocks wandering around the grounds, and gorgeous views of the city from the defensive towers. Leave a little time to explore the camera obscura.

Originally featured in[The Lisbon Guide](link_9)

[![Image 6: Independente Principe Real](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/independente-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/the-independente-hotel [link_11])

[Independente Principe Real](link_11)

83 Rua Sao Pedro de Alcantara, Bairro Alto

Part hotel, part hostel, the Independente feels a little bit like Portugal's version of the Ace. While we wouldn't recommend the hostel rooms unless you're on a tight budget, the suites are lovely, with memorable design quirks like vintage colored leather chairs, bedside lamps made from plumping pipes, and the coolest tile floors in the bathrooms. Be prepared, though, that rooms this reasonable come at the expense of a few amenities—there's no room service, and no mini bar. Not that you'd need one, though, as the food scene is unsurprisingly a huge part of the draw—The Decadente is one of Lisbon's coolest restaurants, and the rooftop bar, The Insólito, is perpetually full of locals grabbing post-work drinks.

[![Image 7: Memmo Alfama](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Alfama-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/memmo-alfama [link_12])

[Memmo Alfama](link_12)

27 Tv. Merceeiras, Alfama

Located in an ancient courtyard in the city’s historic area of Alfama, Memmo Alfama was one of the first boutique hotels in the area, and is still one of the best hotels in Lisbon. From the cozy living room check-in, to its forty-two rooms with amazing views, every inch of the place is intimate and relaxing. The terrace and pool, which also boast incredible views of the river and surrounding city, is the perfect spot for a glass of wine. Plus, the property is only minutes from downtown, and the famous yellow tram (a great way to explore the city) stops nearby, too.

[![Image 8: Memmo Príncipe Real](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/MemmoPrincipeReal2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/memmo-principe-real [link_13])

[Memmo Príncipe Real](link_13)

56 Rua D. Pedro V, Príncipe Real

Hotelier Rodrigo Machaz's third property is set on the top of a hill in the decidedly cool Príncipe Real neighborhood, giving it both a full-circle view of the city (best viewed from the open-air patio of their rooftop bar) and incredible access to some of Lisbon's best shopping and restaurants. Machaz's style is laid back, intimate—only 41 rooms here—and experience-focused, but that doesn't mean his properties skimp on luxury. In addition to the stunning rooftop pool, the hotel is known for high-touch, attentive service, including a concierge with the best recommendations we've come across. Room décor is minimalist but textured, with fur throws at the foot of the bed, floor-to-ceiling paneled headboards, and sleek limestone bathrooms. Leave time for drinks and cocktails at the excellent on-site bar and restaurant.

[![Image 9: Olissippo Lapa Palace Hotel](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/lapa-palace-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/lapa-palace [link_14])

[Olissippo Lapa Palace Hotel](link_14)

4 Rua do Pau de Bandeira, Lapa

Located on a hilltop in the Lapa District of Lisbon, this historic 19th-century palace-turned-hotel offers stunning views of the Tagus River just a short drive from central Lisbon. The hotel was completely renovated in 2003, yet retains much of the timeless charm it had when it was originally built 170 years ago. You can opt for views of the river, or the regal garden and pool; each room or suite features equally impressive décor that varies from Art Deco to colonial to neo-classic styling.

[![Image 10: The One Palácio da Anunciada](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/h10_8-3-19_Piscina-de-di%CC%81a_0038.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenida-de-la-libertad/one-palacio-da-anunciada [link_15])

[The One Palácio da Anunciada](link_15)

R. das Portas de Santo Antão 112-134, Avenida da Liberdade

The One Palácio da Anunciada is one of those gorgeously decrepit sixteenth-century palaces that’s had a contemporary vibrancy breathed back into its hallways—while maintaining the integrity of its past. The grand blush marble staircase that sweeps up from the ornate lobby feels all of 400-plus years old, but the guest rooms belong to 2019. Big beds, bigger bathrooms, and Nespresso machines fill the cool, creamy interiors. The spa area is small but mighty with stellar massages and facials on offer alongside an indoor plunge pool and a steam room. High up at the hotel’s crown is the real reason you came here. The hotel’s outdoor pool seems to hover above the city—a rare indulgence in the capital. The surrounding daybeds make the perfect vantage point from which to take in the detailed azulejo (tin-glazed, ceramic tilework) cladding and frescoes on the surrounding buildings.

[![Image 11: Palacio Ramalhete](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Palacio-Ramalhete-5.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/palacio-ramalhete [link_16])

[Palacio Ramalhete](link_16)

92 Rua das Janelas Verdes, Lapa

Situated in an exclusive residential section of Lisbon's Lapa District, staying in this small boutique hotel feels like staying in an 18th-century private home, with all of the perks of a modern hospitality. The palace’s secret passageways are fun to explore; the beautiful outdoor pool and bar is the perfect place to unwind at the end of the day, and a generous breakfast buffet is great to help you start the next. Note: If you’re staying here during a busy season, it's best to head to the pool on the earlier side to claim a spot.

[![Image 12: Pestana Palace](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Pestana-2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/pestana-palace [link_17])

[Pestana Palace](link_17)

54 Rua Jau, Belém

Once the estate of a cocoa baron, the Pestana Palace has been converted into a hotel and brought back to its former glory, which greets you immediately in the form of an opulent stained glass entryway and the estate's surrounding tropical gardens. Guests get the royal experience here, free to lounge in the indoor and outdoor pools, or dine in the two restaurants that serve Portuguese cuisine with a French twist. While the grounds feel private a secluded, the hotel is near the center of town—it's just seven miles from the Lisbon airport, and close to all the famous monuments of the Belém District.

[![Image 13: Santa Clara 1728](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/SantaClara17281.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/santa-clara-1728 [link_18])

[Santa Clara 1728](link_18)

128 Campo Santa Clara, Alfama

In the center of the city right by the Fiera de Ladra, Lisbon’s flea market, Santa Clara 1728 is a beautiful 18th-century palace that has been transformed into a quiet, romantic sanctuary. Reminiscent of a chic, upscale bed and breakfast, this hotel has six spacious suites and a dining room where the owners (a family who also calls the space home) host delicious dinners open to all guests. Limestone staircases, minimalist wooden furniture, and impressive artwork all complement the beauty of the building itself. Bonus: luxurious, heated bedroom floors, along with views of the Tagus River and National Pantheon.

[![Image 14: A Cevicheria](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/ACevicheria2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/a-cevicheria [link_19])

[A Cevicheria](link_19)

129 Rua Dom Pedro V, Príncipe Real

A Cevicheria is known for putting a Portuguese spin on Peruvian ceviches (and also for its rather dramatic decór element, a large octopus sculpture that looms over the bar). The rest of the space is white-washed and light-filled, making it a clean slate for the order of choice here—ceviches made with fresh fish that chef Kiko Martins hand-selects from Portuguese markets each morning. And if ceviches are the signature dish here, the pisco sours are the signature cocktail—make sure to get at least one for the table.

[![Image 15: A Merendeira](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/a-merendeira-2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/a-merendeira [link_20])

[A Merendeira](link_20)

54 Av. 24 de Julho, Lapa

If you're looking for late night sustenance, this is your spot: It's open until 6am, which is something you might require if you find yourself out dancing late. Specialties here include a nice green soup (caldo verde), and fresh baked rolls filled with chorizo and cheese.

[![Image 16: Alma](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Alma2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/alma [link_21])

[Alma](link_21)

15 Rua Anchieta, Chiado

Henrique Sá Pessoa first opened Alma in 2009—it was his first restaurant, and it catalyzed his career as one of Portugal's few celebrity chefs, opening more restaurants and starring in several cooking shows. Though Alma remained a coveted reservation, Pessoa made the decision to close and relocate the restaurant in 2014, switching up the decór (it's now a warm, mid-century vibe, as though the Eames's decorated an old Portuguese chapel) and recommitting himself to the innovation he was first known for. The gamble paid off—shortly after, the restaurant earned Pessoa his first Michelin star. There are several fixed menus to choose from, although the food can also be ordered a la carte. Either way, have cameras ready, as Pessoa is known for his stunning plating.

[![Image 17: Cervejaria Ramiro](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/16709197939_6dccde61cc_o.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/cervejaria-ramiro [link_22])

[Cervejaria Ramiro](link_22)

1 Av. Almirante Reis, Alfama

Known for serving some of the best seafood in Lisbon, the brightly lit Cervejaria Ramiro is always bustling with foodies—local and foreign alike—clamoring to try the restaurant's famous clams in garlic sauce, grilled giant tiger shrimp, and percebes (goose barnacles), among a host of other amazing options. While it may seem like you won't have room to try anything but the seafood, save some for their prego, a Portuguese steak sandwich—it's said to be the best in the city. Note: unsurprisingly, this place is pretty popular, so if you want to avoid the line (it's first-come, first-served), it's best to try for an early dinner.

[![Image 18: Clube de Jornalistas](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/ClubedeJournalistas5.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/clube-de-jornalistas [link_23])

[Clube de Jornalistas](link_23)

129 Rua Trinas, Lapa

Clube de Jornalistas occupies a converted 18th-century home, but the place to sit is really the gorgeous cobblestone garden/terrace, which is protected on all sides by verdant walls. Both the wine list and the menu are a balance of traditional Portuguese dishes and more international influences—regulars tell us that the lamb burger is the best in town.

[![Image 19: Comida de Santo](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/ComidadeSanto1.png)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alcantara/comida-de-santos [link_24])

[Comida de Santo](link_24)

98 R. 1º de Maio, Alcantara

Mon-Sat: 12:30pm-3:30pm, 7:30pm-1am

Sun: 12:30pm-3:30pm, 7:30pm-12am

Given the historical connection between the countries, it's no surprise that there are a few great Brazilian restaurants in Lisbon. Comida de Santos airs on the kitschy side, but the grilled meats (and the fries they serve them with) are cooked to perfection, and there are a few great seafood picks on the menu, too. Bonus: The lengthy but very complete wine selection is quite reasonable.

Historic landmark

Night view

São Jorge CastleIt is one of the ancient buildings in Lisbon and a major historical monument and tourist attraction in Lisbon. The castle is built onAlfamaThe high point of the area was a fortress when the Moors occupied Lisbon in the Middle Ages. Located on a commanding hillside, its presence can be seen from almost every corner of Lisbon. The castle originally belonged to the earlier Visigoths. After the Moorish invasion, it underwent large-scale expansion, and its walls, up to 8 m thick, still impress with their grandeur today. Here, people can better appreciate the city's architectural art, whether fromAlfamaTo the futuristic castles and drawbridges in the distant city, or in the urbanCarmo churchThe open-air ruins can be seen at a glance. National monument The architectural complex known as Lisbon castle and Lisbon city walls was classified as a national monument under the decree issued on June 16, 1910. The monument is owned by the Portuguese state and was temporarily transferred to Lisbon city hall on September 13, 1934, with the complete transfer finalized on May 31, 1942. On June 8, 1979, the revised terms of transfer for São Jorge Castle were officially enacted. Following the resolution of the Lisbon municipal council in October 1995, São Jorge Castle was placed under the management of the municipal company Empresa de Bairros Históricos de Lisboa (EBAHL). In 2003, this management responsibility was transferred to the municipal company Empresa de Gestão de Equipamentos e Animação Cultural (EGEAC). The site consists of a castle, the ruins of the Alcázar palace, the Plaza de Armas, a spacious viewing platform overlooking the entire city, a museum exhibition area, an archaeological exhibition area, several garden areas, and the city walls. The monument covers an area of approx. 4 hectares, surrounded by a massive perimeter wall and city walls, with one section of the wall coinciding with part of the boundary of Lisbon's old castle. Space and view In the past, there were no trees inside or outside the city walls; even if there were, the quantity was far less than today. In the days when the castle was merely a fortress to be conquered, it was absolutely unacceptable to provide the enemy with any tools for climbing or even setting fires, thereby facilitating their siege. The castle garden was built in the 1950s and is one of the earliest view architecture works in Portugal. Its designer, architect Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles, conceived this garden precisely when the castle completely ceased its military use, aiming to complement the historic site while providing visitors with a highly comfortable leisure area.

### Arco da Rua Augusta Lisbon

I lived in Lisbon for 8 years and never climbed this iconic arch. Biggest mistake of my life. Honestly, I have no excuse. I walked under the Arco da Rua Augusta more times than I can count, always in a rush, always thinking "I'll do it another time." Eight years living in Lisbon. It took a Trip.com booking to finally make me stop and look up. The arch was built to celebrate Lisbon's reconstruction after the catastrophic 1755 earthquake. It took nearly 100 years to complete. Standing at the top, looking out over Praça do Comércio and the Tejo River with the whole city laid out beneath you, you start to understand why it mattered so much to get it right. I booked through Trip.com and it was genuinely straightforward. Found the attraction on the app, picked my time slot, got the voucher on my phone, and exchanged it for the ticket at the entrance in under two minutes. The kind of smooth experience that makes you wonder why travel ever feels complicated. If you're visiting Lisbon and only have a few hours, this is the one. Go late afternoon when the light hits the river and everything turns gold. You'll thank yourself later. Practical info: located at Praça do Comércio in Baixa, right at the waterfront. Book in advance, especially in summer. #LisbonTravel #VisitLisbon #ArcoRuaAugusta #Lisbon #PortugalTravel #TravelEurope ![Image 5: Mirelats](https://ak-d.tripcdn.com/images/0a205424x99ui4jef8A4E_W_100_0_R5_Q90.jpg)Mirelats __ 21

### Lisbon one-day city walk | Old town highlights

No backtracking, about 8–9 km, uphill first then downhill 🚇Transport: Viva Viagem card, valid for metro and trams; if tired, take Bolt or Uber, short rides cost 5–8 euros and are very affordable. 🕘9:00 AM | Start: São Jorge Castle (priority to buy tickets in advance on the official website) Lisbon’s highest point, a Moorish castle overlooking the entire old town with red roofs and the Tagus River. ✅Recommended to arrive right at opening to avoid tour groups. Stay 60–90 minutes. The entire route from here is downhill walking, no need to climb back up. 🕙10:30–11:30 AM | Alfama old town (walk downhill) 🌟Miradouro das Portas do Sol | free Classic panoramic view of red roofs stretching layer upon layer down to the river. 🌟Miradouro de Santa Luzia | 5-minute walk Blue and white azulejo tile murals plus bougainvillea, perfect for photos. The two viewpoints are next to each other. Wander freely through Alfama’s maze of alleys, colorful old houses, and tiled walls to experience the earthquake-surviving old town. 👉On the way, check out Lisbon Cathedral Sé Portugal’s oldest church, optional to enter. 🕛12:00–1:30 PM | Lunch | Baixa downtown Walk downhill to the city center 📍Time Out Market food hall, a one-stop spot for local snacks: green vegetable soup, fried cod balls, grilled octopus. You can also try a pastel de nata egg tart at a street shop and have a glass of Ginjinha cherry liqueur. 🕐1:40–3:30 PM | Baixa-Chiado district 🌟Praça de D. Pedro IV (Rossio Square) The city’s central square with vintage fountains and architecture. 🌟Arco da Augusta + Praça do Comércio Large square by the Tagus River, a landmark rebuilt after the earthquake. Enjoy the river breeze and walk while admiring the April 25 Bridge in the distance. 🌟Convento do Carmo Gothic ruins left by the earthquake, very photogenic; if you don’t want to pay to ride the Santa Justa elevator, you can get a free view of the old town from the nearby rooftop. 🕞4:00–5:30 PM | Bairro Alto upper town 🌟Stroll through the artistic Chiado neighborhood with independent bookstores, vintage shops, and graffiti alleys. Walk to Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara viewpoint A two-level garden viewpoint overlooking the castle, red roofs, and river. It’s one of Lisbon’s best sunset spots, so arrive early to claim a spot. 🕠6:00–8:00 PM | Sunset + night Wait at the viewpoint for the golden sunset as the sun spreads over the old town’s red roofs 🌇. Then explore Bairro Alto’s alleys, known for its lively bars at night. 🍤Must-try foods Pastel de nata Portuguese egg tart: the original Belém shop is the top choice, sprinkled with cinnamon and powdered sugar Bacalhau salted cod: hundreds of recipes, Portugal’s national dish Ginjinha cherry liqueur: a sweet cherry liquor served in edible chocolate cups, available at many old town stalls Tips: Tipping is not mandatory in Portugal. If satisfied, 5–10% is appreciated. If a street vendor helps you take photos or gives directions, they may ask for a tip afterward. Politely decline if you don’t want to tip.  ![Image 7: HEAVEN HARRELL](https://ak-d.tripcdn.com/images/1mi6w12000b8cx3yp6E21_W_100_0_R5_Q90.jpg)HEAVEN HARRELL __

### Lisbon: The Side of the City I Almost Missed

Lisbon is full of famous viewpoints and colorful streets, but I found some of my favorite moments when I wandered beyond the usual tourist route. I started at Mouraria, where narrow lanes, tiled buildings, tiny restaurants, and local life made the neighborhood feel much more authentic than the busy areas around Baixa. I loved simply walking without checking the map every few minutes. Then I headed to LX Factory, a former industrial complex transformed into a creative hub filled with shops, cafés, art, and restaurants. The old factory atmosphere mixed with modern creativity gave it a completely different personality. My third discovery was Jardim do Torel, a small hillside garden where I could sit quietly and look across Lisbon’s rooftops. It was the kind of place I would have easily walked past if I hadn’t been exploring slowly. I still visited Belém Tower, Jerónimos Monastery, São Jorge Castle, Praça do Comércio, Alfama, Santa Justa Lift, and Miradouro da Senhora do Monte, but these three places showed me a more relaxed Lisbon and that was the side I enjoyed most. #lisbon #portugal   Rani Mamahit __ 9

### Lisbon | At the edge of the Eurasian continent, write a gentle poem between the mountains and the sea

Just saying its name feels like your tongue touches the slightly salty breeze of the Atlantic Ocean. If the city had a color, Lisbon would definitely be— the golden yellow of egg tarts🌕 the deep blue of the sea🌊 brushed with a thin layer of honey from the sunset✨ — 🚃 In the morning, you’re awakened by the clanging of trams Walking up the stone steps, the air still carries dew and the scent of coffee Tram 28 is like an old yellow fish slowly weaving through Alfama’s steep alleys I simply jump off, letting myself get lost in the winding lanes Every wall tells a story Blue tiles form waves and white doves Some glaze has peeled away Revealing the warm color of clay Like wrinkles on an old face Footnotes gently left by time📖 — 🏰 Climb up to the São Jorge Castle viewpoint The whole of Lisbon spreads out beneath you— Rust-red roofs cascade from the hillside down to the Tagus River White walls dazzle under the midday sun The April 25 Bridge spans the river On the opposite bank, the statue of Christ opens his arms as if to embrace the city’s gentleness The wind blows in from the river mouth, carrying the scent of the sea, fluttering the edges of clothes I lean against the weathered castle wall Suddenly, time feels light here So light it’s like a piece of silk you can fold at will🍃 — 🥧 In the afternoon, it’s all about Belém The cloisters of Jerónimos Monastery play with light and shadow Stone columns carved with vines and shells, delicate as lace And next door, the egg tart shop— Freshly baked Pastel de Nata The crisp crust cracks like piano keys The custard filling burns the tongue Sweet with a hint of caramel bitterness Paired with an espresso dusted with cinnamon☕ Sitting by the roadside watching passersby At that moment, happiness feels just like this💛 — 🌅 At dusk, I rush back to the São Pedro viewpoint The sun slowly sinks into the Atlantic The sky shifts from orange to rose to deep indigo The whole city bathes in twilight Like a softly hummed Portuguese ballad Lazy, a little sad, yet warmly comforting fado🎵 Lights flicker on in the distance First like scattered stars, then joining into a river of warm yellow light Suddenly, I recall Pessoa’s verse— “My heart is slightly larger than the entire universe.” In Lisbon, between mountains and sea You feel, in a single moment, both Your own smallness and vastness — 🌙 Night deepens, the trams have long stopped I walk slowly back, shadows stretched by street lamps Footsteps echo alone on the cobblestones Yet it doesn’t feel lonely Lisbon is like an understanding old friend Calm and unhurried, accompanying you through the day’s shifting light What I take away are just A few shards of blue tile A hint of egg tart sweetness And sleeves full of sea breeze Some gentleness that will stay in the heart for a long time Like the water of the Tagus River, quietly Flowing toward a never-ending horizon   Olivia.Perry@79 __

🇵🇹 First stop: Rossio Square → Santa Justa Elevator 🚶‍♀️Transport: 3-minute walk ⏰Recommended visit time: 30 minutes This is truly Lisbon’s iconic landmark! This neo-Gothic iron elevator is definitely worth visiting💘 From the top, enjoy a 360° unobstructed view of the old town’s red roofs, a postcard-worthy scene📸 🔥Tip: Buying a combo ticket is more cost-effective~ It’s best to go before 9 AM to avoid crowds! · --------- 🌆 Second stop: Santa Justa Elevator → Castelo Square 🚶‍♀️Transport: 8-minute walk A super artsy, off-the-beaten-path square~ Sit by the fountain, daydream, and soak up the sun while enjoying Lisbon’s slow pace of life☕️ 📸Photo spot: The silhouette of São Jorge Castle is behind you Sunlight on the old city walls feels especially warm · --------- 🇵🇹 Third stop: Castelo Square → Belém Tower 🚌Transport: Tram 15, about 20 minutes 🎫Admission: €6 (available on Trip.com) This 500-year-old fortress is amazing!!! Come here at sunset and watch the whole tower turn golden—truly magical🌅 🍪Must try: Nearby Belém egg tarts (fábrica de Pastéis de Belém) The authentic Portuguese egg tarts are absolutely delicious!!!   ashford.sullivan.beckham __   
*     
### Lisbon, Portugal 🇵🇹

A city of colourful trams, hilltop castles, and breathtaking views over the Tagus River. ✨ Explored Sao Jorge Castle, where the ramparts offer spectacular panoramic views across Lisbon's red rooftops, before riding the Tram through the city's historic neighbourhoods. Visited the magnificent Lisbon Cathedral and the stunning Jeronimos Monastery, masterpieces of Portugal's Age of Discovery. Stopped at the Monument to the Discoveries, honouring explorers such as Christopher Columbus and Vasco da Gama, admired the historic Belem Tower, and walked beneath the grand Rua Augusta Arch, the city's iconic triumphal arch leading into the lively Praca do Comerciod. No visit to Lisbon is complete without trying the world-famous pastel de nata, Portugal's iconic custard tart. Lisbon is a city where history, culture, incredible food, and unforgettable viewpoints await around every corner. #Lisbon #Portugal #SaoJorgeCastle #Tram28 #BelemTower #PastelDeNata #MonumentToTheDiscove ries #RuaAugustaArch #TravelPhotography #Wanderlust #lostpanda ✈️📸  Lost Panda __   
*     
### Measure Lisbon's Old Town on Foot

Lisbon's Old Town mainly consists of four historic districts: Baixa, Chiado, Bairro Alto, and Alfama. It is recommended to split the itinerary into morning and afternoon sessions, taking about 6-7 hours in total. --- 🗺️ Classic Route Overview Morning: Baixa + Chiado Gentle terrain, perfect for starting a day of strolling 1. Rossio Square (Praça do Rossio) The central square of Lisbon, featuring distinctive black and white wave-patterned pavement. The National Theatre (Teatro Nacional D. Maria II) is located here, and in the alleys to the north, you'll find the famous Ginjinha bars, serving a traditional cherry liqueur loved by locals. 2. Santa Justa Lift (Elevador de Santa Justa) A neo-Gothic iron elevator just a 3-minute walk away, built by a student of the Eiffel Tower's designer. If the queue is short (usually 20-30 minutes), you can ride to the top for a panoramic city view; if the line is too long, it's recommended to just take photos from outside. 3. Carmo Square (Largo do Carmo) and Carmo Convent (Convento do Carmo) Gothic ruins preserved after the 1755 earthquake, with the roof collapsed and never restored, making it one of Lisbon's most striking historical sites. The convent houses an archaeological museum. 4. Chiado Square (Chiado) Known as Lisbon's "cultural heart," filled with elegant cafés, bookstores, and theaters. The famous poet Fernando Pessoa was a regular at the Brasileira café located here. 5. Camões Square (Praça Luís de Camões) At the border of Chiado and Bairro Alto, named after the author of "The Lusiads," it is a popular gathering spot for young people.
