# A Puglian Getaway, 3 Ways

Written by:Jena Wolfe Published on:July 22, 2026

![Image 1](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/13/puglia2.png)

Photo courtesy of Borgo Egnazia

For our first child-free vacation together in seven years, my husband and I headed to Puglia, the heel of Italy’s boot, in search of _dolce far niente_: the sweetness of doing nothing. When you have small children, and you suddenly find yourselves without them, _doing nothing_ is about as luxurious as it gets. And because we didn’t have little legs in tow, we decided to divide our trip into three very different styles of vacationing, packing up and relocating every few nights, tasting life at a classic masseria, a converted monastery, and a full-service luxury resort.

## The Masseria

Our first stop: Masseria Trapana. Masserias—traditional Italian farmhouses designed as miniature fortresses enclosing courtyards and gardens—are one of the signature styles of life in Puglia, and many have now been converted into boutique hotels, as well as working farms and restaurants.

Hidden beyond a long dirt road, [Masseria Trapana](https://www.trapana.com/en/) is the kind of place that encourages you to slow down. Lemon and fig trees shade the gardens, cicadas sing from sunrise to sunset, and a soundtrack of 50’s hits and mellow contemporary music drifts quietly across the property. The intimate, nine-room masseria includes an infinity pool, a subterranean hydrotherapy pool housed in a former olive oil mill, a restaurant, a fire pit, and a 16th-century chapel, all painstakingly restored by Australian owner and former marketing executive Rob Potter-Sanders before its 2015 opening.

![Image 2](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/15/masseria24.png)

Photos courtesy of Masseria Trapana

Our suite—a stunning bedroom and living room with 18-foot ceilings—was attended to like clockwork: fresh laundry appeared in the closets after breakfast, and homemade cookies on our pillows at turndown service. And yet we never saw a soul.

“The best masserias are the ones where the owners are present,” one of our fellow guests, a Puglia travel expert, told us over rosé by the pool. Potter-Sanders, who designed the hotel himself, divides his time between the masseria and his native Sydney, and has imparted the space with his own Australian sensibilities: there’s a burger with pineapple on the lunch menu, vegemite at the breakfast buffet, and Aesop bath products in every washroom.

Food at Trapana was simple and fresh and served on a beautiful terrace, though the warm waitstaff were more memorable than the dishes themselves. “Can we have our gelato inside so we can FaceTime our son?” we asked during our only dinner on the property. “Of course,” our server said. “This is your house.”

![Image 3](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/15/masseria2.pn)

Photos courtesy of the author

In addition to ample time by the pool, we spent an afternoon wandering Lecce, the “Florence of the South,” fueled by caffè leccese—espresso poured over ice and sweetened with almond syrup—and a memorable lunch of burrata, crispy artichokes, and honey at [Doppio Zero.](https://www.instagram.com/doppiozero_lecce/?hl=en) We capped it off with a scoop of [Agricola's](https://www.instagram.com/agricolagelaterialecce/) signature goat's milk gelato. With bougainvillea spilling over balconies and jasmine climbing limestone walls, Lecce feels less like a tourist destination than a city going about its daily life. Just don't expect to shop between 1 and 4 p.m. when everything shuts down for the daily _riposo._

## The Converted Monastery

From Masseria Trapana, we drove 45 minutes south to [Il Convento di Santa Maria di Costantinopoli](https://www.ilconventopuglia.com/), in Marittima. Upon arrival, we were greeted by Athena McAlpine—an Irish-born, London-raised Greek and the owner and designer of the Convento—and her giant White Swiss Shepherd, Leo.

McAlpine toured us through the courtyard (replete with folk art and African sculptures), through the long hallways with custom cabinetry, tables, stools, and chairs holding hundreds, no _thousands_, of books, on to the pool and gardens, the communal kitchen (“help yourself”) and tantalizing sitting areas, both indoor and out. Notably, our “private bathroom” was across the hall from our room—“streaking distance!” our hostess told us with a mischievous smile. “Ok,” Athena said at the end of the tour. “You’ve got the keys, you saw the pool, here’s the bottle opener. That’s pretty much it.”

![Image 4](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/15/convento2.png)

Photos courtesy of Il Convento di Santa Maria di Constantinopoli

The design is maximalist, to be sure, but there is a careful resting place for every book, tapestry, and sculpture. Athena, who restored the monastery with her late husband, Alistair McAlpine—the former editor-in-chief of _The World of Interiors_—described their partnership simply: he was "the builder, the collector, the Renaissance man." She was the "editor, straightener, organizer."

We settled into life at the Convento with ease. Mornings at the communal breakfast table were a feast of fresh focaccia, pastries, homemade granola, fruit, and pressed juices, from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. Just like at home, where everyone inevitably gathers in the kitchen, we found ourselves lingering by the refrigerator—after pouring a caffè leccese from a pre-batched bottle—chatting with our fellow guests, all artists and creative types, and with Athena.

If you wish to partake, lunch is served at 2 p.m., dinner at 9 p.m. There is no menu; this is not a restaurant. Pierluigi, the cook, is more like your uncle who is whipping something up for dinner, and it’s going to be very good. We greedily ate every delicious plate put in front of us.

![Image 5](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/15/convento1.pn)

Photos courtesy of Il Convento di Santa Maria di Constantinopoli

The Convento, with just eight bedrooms, is not your typical luxury hotel. “Someone once said we’re like Vegemite,” Athena told me. “You either love it or you hate it.” The staff feels more like family members, happy to help, but they’re busy, too, and fending for oneself is encouraged. Your bed will be made, your bathroom tidied, but you will be tending to your own luggage here. And, perhaps most notable for some: there is no air conditioning.

A hand-drawn map, tacked onto the fridge with magnets, depicted our seaside itinerary: boating at Castro Marina, a dip at Acquaviva, another swim at Tricase Porto followed by aperitivo at Tricase Bar Balboa, a _bed and brolly_ at Athena’s preferred _lido_, Elite.

The sea was clean, cool, and full of caves to explore. In the south of Puglia, it’s all about the clear blue water, the rocky beaches, and umbrella-lined lidos, a Slim Aarons photo come to life. We washed each day down with more Campari spritzes than I could count.

I guess I love Vegemite because I could spend a month—or six—at the Convento. I want to sit in every tiny chair, to view the courtyard, the pool, the gardens, from all angles, behind every prickly cactus. I want to slowly thumb through the books that Athena pulled out for me, like _Writer’s Houses_ by Francesca Premoli-Droulers. “Collecting is a form of addiction,” she admitted. “My extravagance could know no bounds.” I’d need a year, a lifetime maybe, to satisfy my itch to explore this rich world, this dream state of a property that Athena has created.

## The Luxury Resort

It was a bit of a culture shock to go from the quiet, charming convento — easily among the most unique properties I’ve ever visited—to a 45-acre luxury resort like [Borgo Egnazia](https://www.borgoegnazia.com/), a nearly two-hour drive back north. Built from the ground up and opened in 2010 by the Melpignano family, Borgo Egnazia is designed to look and feel like an idealized Puglian village, with winding streets, courtyards, piazzas, and multiple neighborhoods, all constructed from local limestone and featuring artisanal craftsmanship. The amenities are endless: three pools, multiple restaurants, a world-class spa, a beach club, a wellness program, tennis courts, golf, kids’ clubs and more.

It’s yesteryear for the staff, too, who wear traditional linen dresses, belted at the waist for a look that is less uniform than costume. As we strolled through the “town square” —giant, prop-like baskets filled with almonds, lemons, and decorative water bottles in every corner—I couldn’t help but feel like I was walking through a film set. Nights are more theatrical and, arguably, more beautiful, as the entire village is lit with thousands of candles.

![Image 6](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/15/borgo1.png)

Photos courtesy of Borgo Egnazia

The ambiance may be divisive, but there is no argument that the food at Borgo Egnazio is excellent. Dinner at Cala Masciola, the seaside restaurant, included a fresh sea bass—hand-selected from the day’s catch—grilled, with a classic Mediterranean sauce of olives, tomatoes, olive oil, and capers. Also notable was the breakfast buffet, which had enough food for an army of gourmands, including a large gluten-free table with homemade breads, pastries, and packaged snacks.

One could easily spend a week at Borgo with a different daily itinerary. I would happily make my way through every treatment on offer at the stunning [Vair Spa](https://vairspa.com/en/home-en/). But my husband can’t be confined anywhere for long (even a 45-acre hotel village), so we rented a 1974 Alfa Romeo Spider from [Puglia Auto Classica](http://pugliautoclassica.it/) and took it for a spin to nearby Alberobello. A charming little town, Alberobello is famous for its _trulli_—whitewashed limestone houses topped with conical stone roofs. It was nearly 90 degrees and the historic center was jam-packed with tourists—but the storybook rooftops are worth seeing. Even if you do little more than wander the winding streets with gelato, it's the kind of place you'll want to photograph from multiple angles.

![Image 7](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/media/2026/07/15/borgo2.png)

Photos courtesy of Borgo Egnazia

The drive back—with the top down, ancient olive groves blurring past, and quiet country roads stretching ahead—was one of my favorite memories of the entire trip. Each of our three stays had offered its own fantasy—from a whitewashed masseria to a time-traveling borgo to a glamorous seaside escape—and the vintage Alfa felt like the perfect final act, like something straight out of a Bond movie. The kids were at home, but I guess we all like playing pretend sometimes.

![Image 1: Tourists at a stone tower of the Moorish Castle in Sintra, with flags of Portugal and Saudi Arabia flying nearby.](https://cdn.shortpixel.ai/spai/q_lossy+w_1120+to_auto+ret_img/www.lisboacard.org/wp-content/uploads/moorish-castle-sintra-tower-flags-1758169641.jpg)

# Castle of the Moors Tickets

Conquer ancient Moorish walls with spectacular views over Sintra.

Hidden gem Great for couples Historic landmark

### The Moorish Castle Tickets

[**Castle of the Moors: Entry Ticket + Optional Audio Guide**](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-p975020/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tf_p975020)

If you’re visiting just the castle, the basic entry ticket gets you into the Moorish Castle with an optional audio guide. You’ll have plenty of time to explore the ancient walls and soak in those famous panoramic views over Sintra and the Atlantic coast.

[**Castle of the Moors: Skip The Line Ticket & Guided Tour**](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-skip-the-line-and-guided-tour-p1096623/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tf_p1096623)

The guided tour includes a one-hour walk with an English or Portuguese-speaking guide. It’s only €3.80 more than the basic ticket, and you’ll learn about the castle’s history from the Moorish period through to its 19th-century restoration. The guides know the best photo spots too.

[**🏰 Sintra Combo: Pena Palace, Moorish Castle, Quinta da Regaleira**](https://www.getyourguide.com/lisbon-l42/lisbon-sintra-tour-to-pena-palace-castle-and-regaleira-t551556/?partner_id=FENKESD&utm_medium=online_publisher&cmp=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tf_t551556)

Many visitors combine the Moorish Castle with Pena Palace, Quinta da Regaleira, and Sintra town. The private BMW tour (€325 per person, 8 hours) handles all the logistics – transportation between sites, skip-the-line access, and a guide who knows the area inside out. It’s pricier, but when you factor in transport costs and time saved, it makes sense for a special trip.

## Benefits

![Image 2: View of the Moorish Castle walls in Sintra.](https://cdn.shortpixel.ai/spai/q_lossy+w_726+to_auto+ret_img/www.lisboacard.org/wp-content/uploads/moorish-castle-sintra-overlook-1758169638.jpg)cellar-door/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/sintra-portugal-may-2016-castle-moors-sintra-portugal-241995458.html)

*   Stroll along crumbling medieval ramparts as you trace Sintra’s history stone by stone.
*   Soak in bird’s-eye views of Sintra’s other major landmarks – Pena Palace, Quinta de Regaleira Estate, and lush Sintra forests – from the castle’s high vantage points.
*   Skip the ticket line and head straight to the walls when you pre-book online, giving you more time to explore.

## Tickets & Prices

Sintra’s Moorish Castle has two types of visits you can pre-book: self-guided and expert-led.

**[Self-guided Moorish Castle tickets](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-skip-the-line-and-guided-tour-p1096623/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tl_p1096623-1)** let visitors move at their own pace, stopping to take in the medieval setting or the sweeping views of Sintra as long and as often as they want. There’s even a free Zoomguide audio app that will tell you about different parts of the castle as you come to them.

**[Expert-led Moorish Castle tours](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-skip-the-line-and-guided-tour-p1096623/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tl_p1096623-2)** add depth through commentary from a knowledgeable guide who can bring the castle’s 9th-century origins to life. This option is ideal if you want structured insights, historical anecdotes, and the chance to ask questions that deepen your understanding of the castle.

[Check Availability](https://www.tiqets.com/en/castelo-dos-mouros-sintra-tickets-l146205/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_ca)

## Plan Your Visit

### Opening Hours

| Day | Opening Hours | Last Entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday – Sunday | 9:30 – 18:00 | 17:30 |

Last ticket and last admission at 17:30. Hours are often extended until 20:00 during Summer months, but make sure to verify in advance if you’re planning to go later.

The best time of day to visit the castle is right at opening time. The morning has the coolest weather in Sintra all year round, and, unlike other landmarks in Sintra, The Moorish Castle does not have many trees and shelters that will shade you from the sun during your trip.

### Getting There

From Lisbon, the easiest way to reach Sintra is by train on the **Sintra Line (CP)**, which departs every 30 minutes until 23:00 from Rossio, Oriente, or Entrecampos stations. The journey takes around 40 minutes.

Once at Sintra Station, you have a few options to reach The Moorish Castle:

Method Travel Time (incl. waits)Directions Notes
Taxi 15 mins Taxis are waiting in front of the station; ask one to take you to The Moorish Castle entrance.Fast and convenient; pricier than other options, especially in peak season.
Bus 25-40 mins Board the 434 “Circuito da Pena” bus and get off at The Moorish Castle stop Affordable and leaves every 15 mins; can be crowded in summer, sometimes with long queues.
Walking 50-65 mins uphill From the station, follow signs via historic center and forested paths to castle Free and scenic wooded path; steep climb, best for fit visitors who enjoy hiking.

### Map & Address (Location)

#### Castelo dos Mauros

![Image 3: Map of Castelo dos Mauros](blob:http://localhost/308dba39ab209b92ded169796cce9f4a)

2710-405 Sintra, Portugal · [Google Maps](https://maps.google.com/?q=38.792556,-9.3893376)

### Accessibility

The Moorish Castle is great for visitors with mobility issues for a few reasons:

*   A few handicap parking spaces are located near the entrance.
*   It is also the only one of Sintra’s major landmarks that allows dogs.
*   Manual wheelchairs are available at the ticket office. Visitors can rent one for free for 90 minutes of use.
*   Almost all areas of the castle are wheelchair-accessible. Most of the stone stairways are fitted with ramps or wheelchair lifts, and the castle walls are reachable by elevator. Maps at the ticketing office suggest a specific route to take through the castle to fully utilize the amenities.
*   Lots of the surfaces on the grounds are steep or uneven, but the ticketing desk loans out traction equipment that wheelchair users can employ to navigate the difficult terrain.
*   The gift shop, cafe, and restrooms at The Moorish Castle are also wheelchair-accessible.

### Etiquette

*   Stay on marked paths and ramparts – the parts of the castle that have not been reinforced are fragile.
*   Keep noise down at viewpoints – don’t disturb the castle’s serenity.
*   Respect the ruins – don’t touch or sit on fragile walls.
*   Be patient at bottlenecks – the walls only fit one-way traffic in spots; wait your turn instead of forcing past.
*   Secure your belongings – the walls can get seriously windy; secure hats, scarves, and even phones so they don’t fly off the ramparts.

## What to See & Do

### **Second Ring of Walls**

![Image 4: Tourists at the Moorish Castle in Sintra.](blob:http://localhost/de9d42c096e8a73885db044a60976344)
Even more than anywhere else in The Moorish Castle, strolling along the outer walls feels like walking through a medieval fantasy tale. The walls are rough and uneven, with ferns and ivy spilling through cracks.

### **Silos**

Peer inside these round pits in the ground and you’ll see smooth, cylindrical hollows carved into the rock and furnished with ancient-looking stone containers and tools. The silos are cool and shadowy, reminders of how supplies were once tucked safely below the earth.

### **Church of São Pedro de Canaferrim**

![Image 5: Church of São Pedro de Canaferrim, a small stone church with a wooden upper facade, nestled among trees at the Moorish Castle in Sintra.](blob:http://localhost/d4fd010b1ce0bc50b9ccecdc96e0e095) BY-SA 4.0 InternationalGualdimG/[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Igreja_de_S%C3%A3o_Pedro_de_Canaferrim_12.jpg)

You’ll step from the wind and brightness of the ramparts and through a sturdy stone archway into a hushed, sheltered interior at this small church. Neither the exterior nor interior is lavish, but it feels like a sanctuary in the center of the busy castle; the air is cool, dim, and still, with a few panels explaining the church’s history.

### **Tomb & Christian Medieval Necropolis**

Even more so than the adjacent Church, the air in the Tomb & Christian Necropolis feels _thick_ and _humid_. The main reason is that the inside area is full of soil and greenery that add more moisture to the surroundings.

The graves and accompanying markers are simple—no towering crosses or ornate tombs, just faint outlines in the earth and the occasional small stone. They add a solemn layer to the visit, a reminder that the site once became not just a refuge, but a final resting place.

### **Arms Square**

![Image 6: Tourists at a stone tower of the Moorish Castle in Sintra, with flags of Portugal and Saudi Arabia flying nearby.](blob:http://localhost/ee9cd45a10f0141c3e44ad11af23b9e0)sepavone/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/moorish-castle-of-sintra-56136085.html)

The Royal Tower was a favorite retreat of King Ferdinand II.

This square in the center of the castle is a welcome open space after all the narrow stairways and passages. The floor is rough, gravelly, and open to the sky, and often filled with other visitors taking a break. The square was where people once gathered for safety during attacks on the areas around the castle, and now it’s the castle’s natural pause point.

### **Door of Betrayal**

The Door of Betrayal was built into the least-used part of the castle ramparts as a last resort escape hatch to the outside. It’s an unassuming black wooden gate that a lot of visitors miss, but knowing the heavy history behind it makes it an exciting landmark.

### **Towers & Viewpoints**

![Image 7: Stone battlement at the Moorish Castle in Sintra.](blob:http://localhost/b107239b864b80028f0fcdbbd58e60ae)andreslebedev/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/medieval-castle-castelo-dos-mouros-sesimbra-portugal-48543493.html)

The steps to many of the castle’s towers and highest viewpoints are steep, uneven, and wind-exposed, but reaching the top rewards you with enormous panoramas. Some of the best viewpoints include:

**Viewpoint Name****Height Above Sea Level****What You Can See**
**Royal Tower**412 m / 1352 ft Wide-angle views of Pena Palace; Lisbon on clear days.
**Castle Keep**400 m / 1312 ft The best perspective of the castle itself, looking down over the Arms Square and inner walls.
**Northern Battlements**395 m / 1296 ft The rolling green valleys of Sintra.
**Western Ramparts**390 m / 1280 ft The Atlantic coast, with Cabo da Roca Cape visible in the distance.

## Did You Know That? Facts

1.   Features like the Cistern or the Arms Square were meant to serve as places for people to hide during attacks. Sintra was lucky enough to have a peaceful history, though, so the castle never served its defensive purpose.
2.   Centuries ago, the castle was surrounded by an Islamic settlement. Today, the settlement is gone and The Moorish Castle is one of the rare European castles that is just “stranded” on top of a hill with no town surrounding it.
3.   The Moorish Castle once functioned like a little city, with its own Islamic quarter, Christian church, necropolis, and more all crammed inside the fortress walls.

## Insider Tips

1.   Turn left when you enter – Most visitors instinctively head right and follow the battlements clockwise. If you go left instead, you’ll often find fewer people on the walls and get clearer photo angles.
2.   Catch the morning mist – Arrive early and you might see the castle floating above low-lying fog – an incredible sight.
3.   Pack a light layer, even in summer – The altitude means it’s often cooler and windier here than in central Sintra all year round.

## History (Timeline)

**700s-800s**

Built by the Moors to guard Sintra’s strategic mountain pass and to watch Lisbon’s approaches. Was never actually used.

**1100s-1200s**

Gradually loses military importance as Sintra’s population shifts downhill; parts of the castle fall into disuse.

**1300s-1400s**

Earthquakes and neglect leave the structure partially ruined and entirely abandoned.

**1755**

The Great Lisbon Earthquake causes extensive damage, reducing much of the fortress to rubble.

****1800s****

King Ferdinand II oversees partial restoration, reshaping the ruins into a Romantic-era monument alongside nearby Pena Palace.

******1995******

Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

## FAQs

### Do I need to book in advance?

Not required, but [booking online](https://www.tiqets.com/en/castelo-dos-mouros-sintra-tickets-l146205/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tl_l146205) saves time at the gate and locks in entry on busy days.

### Can I visit Pena Palace and the Moorish Castle on the same day?

Easily. They sit a short ride apart and pair well in one trip. Book [Pena ahead](https://www.lisboacard.org/tickets/pena-palace-park/), since its timed slots fill fast.

### Is the Moorish Castle covered by the Lisboa Card?

The [Lisboa Card](https://www.lisboacard.org/) gets you 15% off your ticket, and the train to Sintra is free.

### How long should I spend there?

About 1 to 1.5 hours for the walls, towers, and viewpoints. Photographers and hikers tend to stay longer.

## Plan Your Visit

### Opening Hours

| Months | Opening Hours | Last Entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jan – Mar | 10:00 – 18:30 | 17:30 |
| Apr – Sep | 10:00 – 19:30 | 17:30 |
| Oct – Dec | 10:00 – 18:30 | 17:30 |

*   Closed 1 January,24, 25 and 31 December.
*   Gift shop: closes at 17:30 daily
*   Café: closes at 18:30
*   Palace, the Chapel and eventual exhibition spaces: close 30 minutes before the garden.

#### Best Times to Visit

*   As early as possible (10:00, opening time) – There are fewer crowds earlier in the morning, allowing a more solitary exploration experience. The weather is also cool and crisp. Sometimes there’s even a magical-feeling morning fog drifting around the estate, especially during wetter winter or spring months.
*   The two hours before closing – The crowds die away late in the day, and the golden light of the warm Sintra sunsets make this the most photogenic time to explore Quinta da Regaleira during summer and autumn months.

### Getting There

If you’re coming from Lisbon, make your way to a green line station and take the line towards Sintra. Trains leave every 30 minutes, and it’s a 45-minute ride from Lisbon to Sintra. From there:

**Method of Transport****Directions****Time****Notes/Benefits**
Taxi/ride hailing Grab a taxi or app ride from outside the train station and ask to be dropped at the Quinta da Regaleira main entrance 5-10 mins Most expensive but quick & door-to-door; narrow streets can slow you in peak times.TIP: Use the local ride-hailing app, Bolt.
Bus From the station, board the Scotturb tourist bus #435 and get off at the stop for Quinta da Regaleira or the historic centre (short walk to the entrance).10-30 mins Cheap and drops you close to the gate; buses leave every 20 minutes.
Walk Google Maps 20-30 mins A charming, scenic walk AND freedom to explore the town.

### Map & Address

#### Quinta da Regaleira

![Image 2: Map of Quinta da Regaleira](blob:http://localhost/07c66a006f0ea1628ae0c4538a659fef)

Quinta da Regaleira, 2710-567 Sintra, Portugal · [Google Maps](https://maps.google.com/?q=38.7963069,-9.3960244)

### Accessibility

Most of the estate is difficult or impossible to navigate with mobility issues. The main attractions, including the Palace, the Regaleira Tower, the underground wells, and the tunnel system all involve steep stairways that aren’t fitted with ramps or elevator alternatives.

There is a parking lot on the grounds and most of the outdoor spaces are navigable in a wheelchair, but many of them are on hills and so may require pushing assistance.

### Etiquette

A few tips to stay respectful at Quinta da Regaleira:

*   Use your indoor voice, even in the outdoor areas. Quinta da Regaleira is a peaceful, atmospheric place, and boisterous groups ruin the vibe. This is especially important in the chapel; remember it’s a sacred space.
*   Stay out of the roped-off areas.
*   Don’t climb on structures or statues, even to pose for a photo.
*   Do not pick plants from the garden
*   If you’re taking photos that include people, ask permission to photograph them first
*   No drones or tripods allowed

## What to See & Do

### Main Gate & Entrance Courtyards

![Image 3: Street-level view of the main entrance to the Quinta da Regaleira Palace in Sintra, with stone walls and a grand staircase.](blob:http://localhost/4114a63a4c02cfa3b40b94c89aa5ea58)mango2friendly/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/quinta-da-regaleira-sintra-107177940.html)

From the entrance on Rua Barbosa du Bocage, go through the large iron gates and start down the smooth stone path. An old brick building with ticketing, an info center, and restrooms will be on your right, and the cafe will be on your left.

The entrance courtyard is a great place for you to orient yourself and set off on your self-guided tour. We’d suggest tackling the landmarks described below in this order:

1.   Gardens
2.   Initiation Well
3.   Unfinished Well
4.   Waterfall Lake
5.   Chapel
6.   Palace
7.   Tower

### Gardens

![Image 4: Aerial view of the lush gardens at Quinta da Regaleira, with the palace partially visible among tall trees and greenery.](blob:http://localhost/156c7ebf2ca725366274f6a912302bca)bennymarty/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/quinta-da-regaleira-223340710.html)

A 30–40 minute stroll through the gardens is the perfect way to ease into Quinta da Regaleira’s enchanting atmosphere.

The cobblestone paths of the gardens twist and climb through dense greenery, winding through sheltered lawns and open terraces with sweeping views of Sintra. Along the way, you’ll pass moss-covered walls of ancient brick, hidden stone staircases, and babbling fountains. Decorative stone benches and architectural flourishes from fairy tales dot the route, as well.

The gardens were deliberately designed to include visual metaphors symbolizing a spiritual journey, so even the landscaping carries layers of meaning.

### Initiation Well & Unfinished Well (Poço Iniciático & Poço Inacabado)

These two adjacent “wells” were never actually used for water; they are both circular chambers dug deep into the earth with staircases built in.

![Image 5: View from the bottom of the spiral Initiation Well at Quinta da Regaleira, with moss-covered stone arches and a circular opening to the sky.](blob:http://localhost/84e2f37579a17480052c368cb6a52682)diegograndi/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/editorial/sintra-portugal-feb-2020-initiation-well-quinta-regaleira-sintra-portugal-620964434.html)

View from the bottom of the spiral Initiation Well.

The Initiation Well is the more elaborate of the two, ringed by an arch-lined staircase spiraling down 27 meters. The theatrical-feeling descent is symbolic of initiation rites and rebirth. It leads into a network of dark tunnels that connect to other corners of the estate. Bring closed-toe shoes and a flashlight!

![Image 6: Moss-covered rock walls and passage openings inside the Unfinished Well at Quinta da Regaleira, viewed from the bottom.](blob:http://localhost/b2d6f42c31c3d86780117c7acf7f46d3)diegograndi/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/editorial/sintra-portugal-feb-2020-interior-unfinished-well-quinta-regaleira-sintra-620964330.html)

Inside the Unfinished Well, viewed from the bottom.

The Unfinished Well is smaller and more “rough around the edges” than its counterpart. Its incomplete state gives it a raw, mysterious vibe that makes it feel dark and ominous.

### Waterfall Lake (Lago de Cascata)

![Image 7: A small waterfall cascading into a lake inside a rocky cave at Quinta da Regaleira, with sunlight filtering through the foliage.](blob:http://localhost/8bfb83a4b73b5082f132d55bd6948af6)WHPics/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/editorial/sintra-portugal-aug-8th-2024-quinta-regaleira-one-principal-tourist-751205260.html)

At arguably the prettiest water feature on the estate, a cave opens onto a small pond with gorgeous aquamarine water and 8 stepping stones leading across. A man-made waterfall trickles into the pool, creating a cool, secluded atmosphere.

You can walk across the stones for the best view of the grotto. Careful, though, because the uneven rocks can get very slippery when wet.

### Regaleira Chapel (Capela da Santíssima Trindade)

![Image 8: The Gothic-style chapel at Quinta da Regaleira with intricate carvings, statues, and sunlight shining through the trees.](blob:http://localhost/18ed501a09700c9972350031b5af34d1)sergoua/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/church-for-prayer-at-quinta-regaleira-portugal-sintra-64710167.html)

The small chapel is filled with intricate frescoes, stained glass, and mosaics that illustrate the palace’s themes of mysticism and faith. The walls of the small but high-ceilinged place also echo sound amazingly well, making the chapel feel like a cathedral. Try visiting when the chapel is quiet to really appreciate the atmosphere.

### Regaleira Palace (Palácio da Regaleira)

![Image 9: The ornate façade of the Quinta da Regaleira Palace in Sintra, Portugal, surrounded by lush gardens and stone staircases.](blob:http://localhost/bd7fbac26571752a39a69645bede4347)homydesign/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/editorial/quinta-da-regaleira-in-sintra-53177455.html)

The palace blends Gothic, Renaissance, and Romantic design features into one ornate residence. Inside, you can explore lavishly furnished rooms, carved wood ceilings, and mind-bogglingly detailed stonework that are the result of boundless imagination + tremendous wealth.

The palace’s balconies and windows also provide panoramic views of the gardens. Allow at least 30–40 minutes here, moving room-to-room at your own pace.

### Regaleira Tower

![Image 10: A round stone tower with decorative battlements and arches nestled in the forest at Quinta da Regaleira, surrounded by trees.](blob:http://localhost/9ec3bf1d2b166a00b45440db92a91e51)Lusoimages/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/editorial/sintra-portugal-july-2015-portal-dos-guardiaes-regaleira-palace-gardens-219770786.html)

Emanating from the palace and stretching above the rest of the estate like Rapunzel’s tower, this is the best vantage point at Quinta da Regaleira. There’s a stone spiral staircase leading up to the top, and it can get very crowded during peak hours since it’s so narrow.

There is so much to explore on the Quinta da Regaleira estate that we couldn’t include all of it! We hit all the big landmarks, but one of the best activities at Quinta da Regaleira is doing some freeform wandering and discovering the hidden nooks and crannies yourself.

## Did You Know That? Facts

1.   Luigi Manini, Quinta da Regaleira’s designer, was originally a set designer for theater and opera. That explains why the estate is so atmospheric and the interiors have such good acoustics.
2.   Most landmarks in Sintra are ancient, but Quinta da Regaleira was just completed in 1910 and made to look old.
3.   Secret passageways beneath the gardens connect Quinta da Regaleira’s major landmarks.

## Insider Tips

1.   Bring a small flashlight (or use your phone).
2.   Use the hilly garden paths. Most visitors stick to the main routes, but the elevated paths give you fantastic views of the palace.
3.   Allow 2-3 hours for your visit.

## History (Timeline)

**Late 1600s–1700s**

The Regaleira family builds the estate, though it didn’t have all the features it now does.

**1892**

Brazilian coffee magnate Antonio Augusto Carvalho Monteiro purchases the property.

**1898–1910**

Architect Luigi Manini adds the palace, chapel, wells, waterfalls, and gardens.

**1940s–1980s**

The estate changes hands several times, eventually falling into partial neglect.

****1997****

The Municipality of Sintra acquires the property, restoring it for public access.

****1998****

Quinta da Regaleira opens to visitors as a cultural and tourist site.

## FAQs

### Do I need to book Quinta da Regaleira in advance?

Not required, but [booking online](https://www.tiqets.com/en/quinta-da-regaleira-tickets-l191293/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--quinta-da-regaleira_mc_tl_l191293) saves a long queue in peak season, and entry runs on timed slots so you won’t wait at the gate.

### Is Quinta da Regaleira included in the Lisboa Card?

Quinta da Regaleira isn’t on the [Lisboa Card](https://www.lisboacard.org/), but the rest of Sintra is well covered. ## How to book cheap flights

*   Fly during the working week   Opting to take your flight during the working week can save you money. Flights departing over this period – especially Tuesdays and Wednesdays – are cheaper, mainly because these days are less popular to travel on. 
*   Have a look at airline websites   Many airline websites have made it simpler to identify the inexpensive days to fly by displaying a "calendar view" booking system. This system allows you to scan prices ranging across the week that you are searching. 
*   Consider flights with less-popular departure times   You may also get a bargain flight if you're willing to fly at an early hour. It may well be less expensive to fly at 6 am than at later times due to that time spot being less popular. The only problem you could face is getting to the airport at this time; make sure that public transport is running if you can't take a taxi or get a lift to the airport. 
*   Find a better price on the Trip.com app   This may sound like I'm stating the obvious, but you'd be surprised at the number of people who settle for a price without first shopping around and doing some research. We suggest you have a look for bargains on the Trip.com app. 
*   Book early instead of waiting until the last minute   Don't get fooled into thinking that last-minute deals are necessarily the best option for cheap flight tickets because they seldom are.  
The smart move is to book early, even as far as a year in advance if that is possible for the flight you require. Flight tickets have a tendency to be cheaper when they are first released – which is normally about a year before the flight – so have a look online as soon as the flights you want are available.  
This is particularly true if you are planning to travel during school holidays or to a destination where a famous event is taking place. These prices will increase rapidly, so book before the masses do.  
The price of a flight may drop again before re-climbing in the last few days before the flight takes off but they also may not. It's not worth the risk of waiting for a drop in prices only to be faced with higher prices for leaving it until the last minute. You also run the risk that the tickets will become sold out before you book yours, especially if it's a popular flight.  
If you're willing to be flexible, which is really the name of the game for cheap flight tickets, then have a look at a flight search engine as it may post flight tickets which get lower in price as the flight time approaches. 
*   Use a credit card in a wiser way   There are a lot of advantages to paying for a flight with a credit card. One advantage is that you are protected when you make bigger purchases. For example, if you spend more than $100 on a flight, you will be covered for a refund if the airline or travel company goes out of business. This will not necessarily be the case if you pay with a debit card so check first. Credit cards are also more useful for spending in a foreign country and give you better exchange rates than you would get with your debit card.  
Certain credit cards will offer you air miles for each sum of money spent, thus saving you a bit more on your flight tickets. They may also give you a certain amount of cashback on the purchase of your flight ticket. 
*   Choose flights with a connection   Booking a flight with a connection is nearly always a cheaper option, especially on longer-haul flights. The best thing to do is to uncheck the "non-stop only" option on your flight booking website's search engine, and have a look to see if the flights shown are any cheaper. However, there is a degree of risk involved in this method of getting cheap air tickets. If one of your earlier flights is delayed, this could mean that you miss a later connecting flight. 
*   Book package holidays which may offer cheap flight tickets   If you book a package holiday, you are likely to get discounts on flights as well as accommodation. This is because travel companies book tickets in such large volumes that they get huge discounts. It is sometimes possible to get a whole holiday for less than the price of a regular flight. 
*   Be aware of hidden costs of cheap flights   Be aware that cheap flight tickets with budget airlines can be deceptive. Very often there can be hidden costs, so check for air taxes, baggage fees, or seat selection costs before you buy. Airlines can also add travel insurance and other features on automatically without checking to see if you want them first.  
Travel light if it's possible. Carry-on baggage is usually free, but be sure to check the regulations on weight limitations first.

Signature city moments: Many visitors say Portugal’s charm reveals itself in tile‑clad facades, steep lanes and river light, with Porto’s sunset from Dom Luís I Bridge repeatedly singled out as a must. In Lisbon, the open‑to‑the‑sky Gothic nave at Carmo Convent is often described as most contemplative around midday. Seasonal timing: Winter (October–March) brings Nazaré’s record‑breaking Atlantic swell, making it prime time for wave watching. In early spring, the Algarve is perfumed by orange blossom as trees flower while last season’s fruit still hangs—an unusual “two seasons on one branch” sight. Food and value: Travelers consistently praise Portugal’s price‑to‑experience ratio, noting full meals from about €8–12 and affordable transit. Warm Pastel de Nata with a dusting of cinnamon, simple seafood (sardines, octopus) and countless Bacalhau dishes are recurring favorites; in Porto, the hearty Francesinha and Port wine tastings add a romantic, local touch, with watercolor‑tube jam recommended as a light, well‑liked souvenir. Practical tips: City travel is easy—walk and trams handle the hills, trains link Porto and Lisbon smoothly, and ride‑hailing is surprisingly cheap. Crowded routes and old quarters can attract pickpockets, so keep bags secure; wear grippy shoes for polished limestone streets, and prebook popular palaces near Lisbon and start early to avoid queues.

Immerse yourself in nature in Madeira, Portugal 🇵🇹 from lush green mountains and seaside cliffs to charming villages and spectacular hiking trails. 📍 Don't miss: Funchal, Pico do Arieiro, Cabo Girão, and the Porto Moniz natural pool. 🌤️ Perfect for nature lovers, photography enthusiasts, and road trips. ✈️ Plan your trip to Madeira and book your flights and accommodation at Trip.com #Madeira #Portugal #TravelPortugal #InternationalTravel #Tripcom ![Image 4: เจ๊นางพาเล๊าะ](https://ak-d.tripcdn.com/images/0a202224x9ag0jpbw227C_W_100_0_R5_Q90.jpg)เจ๊นางพาเล๊าะ __ 3

### I’m a Planner - But I Plan for Freedom

My travel personality is definitely the Planner. Before a trip, I study routes, transport, opening hours and the best times for photography. On our road trip through Portugal, for example, we drove almost 2,000 kilometres, so every overnight stop and major transfer had to fit together. Yet I do not plan because I want to follow a strict checklist. I plan because good preparation gives me more freedom during the journey. If the essential logistics are already solved, I can spend longer at a beautiful viewpoint, wait for better light or change the day when the weather turns. I can enjoy the experience instead of constantly checking how to reach the next place. My planning style has also changed over time. I now leave more breathing room and try not to fill every available hour. A successful itinerary is not the one with the greatest number of attractions. It is the one that makes the trip feel smooth while still leaving space for unexpected discoveries. ### 🇵🇹 Lisbon — A City Bathed in Sunlight, Soul & Stories✨

Perched beside the sparkling Tagus River, Lisbon feels like a beautiful poem written in golden light. ☀️🌊 Its winding cobblestone streets climb through colorful neighborhoods, historic trams glide past pastel-painted buildings, and the sound of Portuguese music seems to drift gently through the evening air. 🎶🏘️ From the charming alleys of Alfama to the grand squares of Baixa, every corner carries a little piece of history. Wander beneath balconies filled with flowers, pause at a quiet viewpoint overlooking the rooftops, and watch the city glow as the sun slowly sinks beyond the horizon. 🌅💛 Lisbon is a city of contrasts—old yet vibrant, peaceful yet full of life, nostalgic yet endlessly alive. It doesn't simply invite you to explore; it invites you to slow down and feel every moment. ✨ Golden streets, soulful melodies, ocean air, and stories hidden in every corner—Lisbon is the kind of city that stays in your heart long after you leave. 🇵🇹❤️ #lisbon #portugal #travelphotography #traveldiaries #cityoflight #historiccity #exploreeurope #culturaltravel#tripmoments #beautifuldestinations #exploreportugal   RufRab __ 9

### Octopus in Portugal: The Must-Try Dish I Ordered Again and Again

Before travelling to Portugal, octopus was not something I would normally consider ordering. It is quite an unusual dish where I live, so the first time I chose it was mainly out of curiosity. That first plate completely changed my plans for the rest of the trip. I enjoyed it so much that whenever I saw octopus on another restaurant menu, I wanted to try it again. What began as a one-time food experiment gradually became one of the dishes I ordered most often in Portugal. The versions varied slightly between restaurants, but the octopus was usually served with potatoes. It is a simple combination, yet it works remarkably well. The mild flavour of the potatoes balances the seafood, while olive oil, garlic and seasoning bring everything together. When prepared properly, octopus has a tender texture and a delicate flavour. Some restaurants served it with a lightly grilled or roasted exterior, adding a little smokiness and contrast. The potatoes were sometimes roasted until golden and sometimes served softer, soaking up the olive oil and juices from the plate. Trying the same dish in several places also became an interesting comparison. The basic ingredients remained familiar, but the texture, seasoning and presentation changed. One restaurant might focus on a beautifully charred tentacle, while another served a more traditional and comforting plate with generous potatoes and olive oil. That consistency was part of the appeal. Even though every version was different, the combination rarely felt overly complicated. Good ingredients and careful preparation were enough. Portugal has many famous foods, from pasteis de nata to bacalhau, but octopus became my personal discovery of the trip. I initially ordered it because it felt unfamiliar. I continued ordering it because it had become one of my favourite meals. If you have never tried octopus before, Portugal is an excellent place to begin. Choose a restaurant specialising in Portuguese cuisine, look for octopus served with potatoes and give it a chance - even if the dish initially seems unusual. ### Lisbon: The Side of the City I Almost Missed

Lisbon is full of famous viewpoints and colorful streets, but I found some of my favorite moments when I wandered beyond the usual tourist route. I started at Mouraria, where narrow lanes, tiled buildings, tiny restaurants, and local life made the neighborhood feel much more authentic than the busy areas around Baixa. I loved simply walking without checking the map every few minutes. Then I headed to LX Factory, a former industrial complex transformed into a creative hub filled with shops, cafés, art, and restaurants. The old factory atmosphere mixed with modern creativity gave it a completely different personality. My third discovery was Jardim do Torel, a small hillside garden where I could sit quietly and look across Lisbon’s rooftops. It was the kind of place I would have easily walked past if I hadn’t been exploring slowly. I still visited Belém Tower, Jerónimos Monastery, São Jorge Castle, Praça do Comércio, Alfama, Santa Justa Lift, and Miradouro da Senhora do Monte, but these three places showed me a more relaxed Lisbon and that was the side I enjoyed most. #lisbon #portugal   Rani Mamahit __ 9

### One Day Trip to Sintra from Lisbon🇵🇹

If you are visiting Lisbon and have one extra day, I really recommend taking a day trip to Sintra. It is not far from Lisbon, but once you arrive, the atmosphere feels completely different. The town is surrounded by green hills, beautiful palaces and some of the most unusual architecture I saw during my trip to Portugal. Getting here is quite easy. From Lisbon, you can take a direct train from Rossio Station to Sintra Station, which takes around 40 minutes. Once you arrive in Sintra, you can continue by local bus to the main attractions. I would recommend starting early because there is actually a lot to see, especially if you want to visit three places in one day like we did. For our day trip, we chose Pena Palace, Quinta da Regaleira and Monserrate Palace. What I really liked was that even though all three are in Sintra, they have completely different characters. 🏰 Pena Palace (Palácio Nacional da Pena) Our first stop was Pena Palace, probably the most famous landmark in Sintra. The palace sits high on the hill and is one of the most important examples of 19th-century Romantic architecture in Portugal. But forget the history for a moment — my first impression was that it looked like a giant LEGO castle! With its bright yellow and red walls, towers, domes, arches and so many different shapes put together, it is colourful, playful and almost unreal. It feels like someone took pieces from different fairytale castles and combined them into one. There are also lots of interesting details to discover as you walk around, including the famous Triton sculpture above one of the gateways. Don’t forget to walk out onto the terraces as well. Because the palace is located high on the hill, the panoramic view from here is beautiful. 🌳Quinta da Regaleira The whole place feels mysterious and a little magical. Instead of simply walking through palace rooms, you can explore gardens, stone towers, tunnels and hidden passages. There is always something around the next corner, so it really feels like you are exploring a fantasy world. The highlight is definitely the famous Initiation Well, a deep circular structure with a spiral staircase running down the inside. You can walk down into it and continue through the underground passages. This was probably the place that gave me the strongest feeling of being inside a fantasy movie — mysterious, unusual and fun to explore. 🌸Monserrate Palace (Palácio de Monserrate) From the outside, I already thought the palace was beautiful. The building is surrounded by greenery and gardens, with its elegant towers and domes standing out among the trees. But once I walked inside, it was even more beautiful. This is the kind of place where you should slow down and look at the details. The arches, columns, ceilings and intricate decorations are beautiful almost everywhere you look. The architecture combines different influences, including Gothic, Moorish and Indian elements, giving the palace a very elegant and exotic feeling. And it is not only the palace itself. The gardens around Monserrate are beautiful too, with plants from different parts of the world and plenty of greenery surrounding the property. I really enjoyed walking around here because the whole place felt peaceful and romantic. #sintra #penapalace #portugal   Giftmetrip __ 5

### Lisbon - Hills and Navigation

Lisbon is a mountain town full of storytelling, and the distance between the old city and the Atlantic Ocean always evokes imagination. On this two-day trip, walk along the stone roads up the hills, slowly feel Portugal’s maritime history, Mediterranean atmosphere and unbeatable sunset views, and finally understand why everyone recommends an in-depth trip to Lisbon. 🗓️Itinerary: Day 1: Alphama Old Town — St. Lucia Observation Deck — St. Jorge Castle Day 2: Jeronimos Monastery—Beren Tower—Sailboat in the evening to watch the sunset Day 1 Highlights: The first stop is Alfama Old Town, an area that retains the most pristine taste of Lisbon. The narrow and winding streets, the walls covered with colored tiles and nostalgic authentic small shops, the aroma of coffee and the ever-present Fado song makes people linger. # Palacio Ramalhete

Lapa, Lisbon, Portugal

![Image 1](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Palacio-Ramalhete-5.jpg)![Image 2](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Palacio-Ramalhete-2.jpg)![Image 3](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Palacio-Ramalhete-3.jpg)![Image 4](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Palacio-Ramalhete-4.jpg)

## why we love it

Situated in an exclusive residential section of Lisbon's Lapa District, staying in this small boutique hotel feels like staying in an 18th-century private home, with all of the perks of a modern hospitality. The palace’s secret passageways are fun to explore; the beautiful outdoor pool and bar is the perfect place to unwind at the end of the day, and a generous breakfast buffet is great to help you start the next. Note: If you’re staying here during a busy season, it's best to head to the pool on the earlier side to claim a spot.

[![Image 5: Independente Principe Real](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/independente-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/the-independente-hotel)

[Independente Principe Real](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/the-independente-hotel)

83 Rua Sao Pedro de Alcantara, Bairro Alto

Part hotel, part hostel, the Independente feels a little bit like Portugal's version of the Ace. While we wouldn't recommend the hostel rooms unless you're on a tight budget, the suites are lovely, with memorable design quirks like vintage colored leather chairs, bedside lamps made from plumping pipes, and the coolest tile floors in the bathrooms. Be prepared, though, that rooms this reasonable come at the expense of a few amenities—there's no room service, and no mini bar. Not that you'd need one, though, as the food scene is unsurprisingly a huge part of the draw—The Decadente is one of Lisbon's coolest restaurants, and the rooftop bar, The Insólito, is perpetually full of locals grabbing post-work drinks.

[![Image 6: Memmo Alfama](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Alfama-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/memmo-alfama)

[Memmo Alfama](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/memmo-alfama)

27 Tv. Merceeiras, Alfama

Located in an ancient courtyard in the city’s historic area of Alfama, Memmo Alfama was one of the first boutique hotels in the area, and is still one of the best hotels in Lisbon. From the cozy living room check-in, to its forty-two rooms with amazing views, every inch of the place is intimate and relaxing. The terrace and pool, which also boast incredible views of the river and surrounding city, is the perfect spot for a glass of wine. Plus, the property is only minutes from downtown, and the famous yellow tram (a great way to explore the city) stops nearby, too.

[![Image 7: Memmo Príncipe Real](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/MemmoPrincipeReal2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/memmo-principe-real)

[Memmo Príncipe Real](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/memmo-principe-real)

56 Rua D. Pedro V, Príncipe Real

Hotelier Rodrigo Machaz's third property is set on the top of a hill in the decidedly cool Príncipe Real neighborhood, giving it both a full-circle view of the city (best viewed from the open-air patio of their rooftop bar) and incredible access to some of Lisbon's best shopping and restaurants. Machaz's style is laid back, intimate—only 41 rooms here—and experience-focused, but that doesn't mean his properties skimp on luxury. In addition to the stunning rooftop pool, the hotel is known for high-touch, attentive service, including a concierge with the best recommendations we've come across. Room décor is minimalist but textured, with fur throws at the foot of the bed, floor-to-ceiling paneled headboards, and sleek limestone bathrooms. Leave time for drinks and cocktails at the excellent on-site bar and restaurant.

[![Image 8: Olissippo Lapa Palace Hotel](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/lapa-palace-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/lapa-palace)

[Olissippo Lapa Palace Hotel](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/lapa-palace)

4 Rua do Pau de Bandeira, Lapa

Located on a hilltop in the Lapa District of Lisbon, this historic 19th-century palace-turned-hotel offers stunning views of the Tagus River just a short drive from central Lisbon. The hotel was completely renovated in 2003, yet retains much of the timeless charm it had when it was originally built 170 years ago. You can opt for views of the river, or the regal garden and pool; each room or suite features equally impressive décor that varies from Art Deco to colonial to neo-classic styling.

[![Image 9: The One Palácio da Anunciada](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/h10_8-3-19_Piscina-de-di%CC%81a_0038.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenida-de-la-libertad/one-palacio-da-anunciada)

[The One Palácio da Anunciada](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenida-de-la-libertad/one-palacio-da-anunciada)

R. das Portas de Santo Antão 112-134, Avenida da Liberdade

The One Palácio da Anunciada is one of those gorgeously decrepit sixteenth-century palaces that’s had a contemporary vibrancy breathed back into its hallways—while maintaining the integrity of its past. The grand blush marble staircase that sweeps up from the ornate lobby feels all of 400-plus years old, but the guest rooms belong to 2019. Big beds, bigger bathrooms, and Nespresso machines fill the cool, creamy interiors. The spa area is small but mighty with stellar massages and facials on offer alongside an indoor plunge pool and a steam room. High up at the hotel’s crown is the real reason you came here. The hotel’s outdoor pool seems to hover above the city—a rare indulgence in the capital. The surrounding daybeds make the perfect vantage point from which to take in the detailed azulejo (tin-glazed, ceramic tilework) cladding and frescoes on the surrounding buildings.

[![Image 10: Pestana Palace](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Pestana-2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/pestana-palace)

[Pestana Palace](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/pestana-palace)

54 Rua Jau, Belém

Once the estate of a cocoa baron, the Pestana Palace has been converted into a hotel and brought back to its former glory, which greets you immediately in the form of an opulent stained glass entryway and the estate's surrounding tropical gardens. Guests get the royal experience here, free to lounge in the indoor and outdoor pools, or dine in the two restaurants that serve Portuguese cuisine with a French twist. While the grounds feel private a secluded, the hotel is near the center of town—it's just seven miles from the Lisbon airport, and close to all the famous monuments of the Belém District.

[![Image 11: Santa Clara 1728](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/SantaClara17281.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/santa-clara-1728)

[Santa Clara 1728](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/santa-clara-1728)

128 Campo Santa Clara, Alfama

In the center of the city right by the Fiera de Ladra, Lisbon’s flea market, Santa Clara 1728 is a beautiful 18th-century palace that has been transformed into a quiet, romantic sanctuary. Reminiscent of a chic, upscale bed and breakfast, this hotel has six spacious suites and a dining room where the owners (a family who also calls the space home) host delicious dinners open to all guests. Limestone staircases, minimalist wooden furniture, and impressive artwork all complement the beauty of the building itself. Bonus: luxurious, heated bedroom floors, along with views of the Tagus River and National Pantheon.

[![Image 12: A Cevicheria](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/ACevicheria2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/a-cevicheria)

[A Cevicheria](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/a-cevicheria)

129 Rua Dom Pedro V, Príncipe Real

A Cevicheria is known for putting a Portuguese spin on Peruvian ceviches (and also for its rather dramatic decór element, a large octopus sculpture that looms over the bar). The rest of the space is white-washed and light-filled, making it a clean slate for the order of choice here—ceviches made with fresh fish that chef Kiko Martins hand-selects from Portuguese markets each morning. And if ceviches are the signature dish here, the pisco sours are the signature cocktail—make sure to get at least one for the table.

[![Image 13: A Merendeira](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/a-merendeira-2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/a-merendeira)

[A Merendeira](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/a-merendeira)

54 Av. 24 de Julho, Lapa

If you're looking for late night sustenance, this is your spot: It's open until 6am, which is something you might require if you find yourself out dancing late. Specialties here include a nice green soup (caldo verde), and fresh baked rolls filled with chorizo and cheese.

[![Image 14: Alma](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Alma2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/alma)

[Alma](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/alma)

15 Rua Anchieta, Chiado

Henrique Sá Pessoa first opened Alma in 2009—it was his first restaurant, and it catalyzed his career as one of Portugal's few celebrity chefs, opening more restaurants and starring in several cooking shows. Though Alma remained a coveted reservation, Pessoa made the decision to close and relocate the restaurant in 2014, switching up the decór (it's now a warm, mid-century vibe, as though the Eames's decorated an old Portuguese chapel) and recommitting himself to the innovation he was first known for. The gamble paid off—shortly after, the restaurant earned Pessoa his first Michelin star. There are several fixed menus to choose from, although the food can also be ordered a la carte. Either way, have cameras ready, as Pessoa is known for his stunning plating.

[![Image 15: Cervejaria Ramiro](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/16709197939_6dccde61cc_o.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/cervejaria-ramiro)

[Cervejaria Ramiro](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/cervejaria-ramiro)

1 Av. Almirante Reis, Alfama

Known for serving some of the best seafood in Lisbon, the brightly lit Cervejaria Ramiro is always bustling with foodies—local and foreign alike—clamoring to try the restaurant's famous clams in garlic sauce, grilled giant tiger shrimp, and percebes (goose barnacles), among a host of other amazing options. While it may seem like you won't have room to try anything but the seafood, save some for their prego, a Portuguese steak sandwich—it's said to be the best in the city. Note: unsurprisingly, this place is pretty popular, so if you want to avoid the line (it's first-come, first-served), it's best to try for an early dinner.

# Castelo de São Jorge

Alfama, Lisbon, Portugal

![Image 1](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge1.jpg)![Image 2](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge5.jpg)![Image 3](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge2.jpg)![Image 4](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge4.jpg)![Image 5](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/CastelodeSJorge3.jpg)

## why we love it

Set on the city's tallest hill (where its Middle-Age inhabitants could best see incoming threats), São Jorge Castle was originally built by the Moors, before it was captured by the Christians who eventually ruled the city. Despite its dramatic history, today, the castle is one of the city's most relaxing and tranquil places—there are peacocks wandering around the grounds, and gorgeous views of the city from the defensive towers. Leave a little time to explore the camera obscura.

Part hotel, part hostel, the Independente feels a little bit like Portugal's version of the Ace. While we wouldn't recommend the hostel rooms unless you're on a tight budget, the suites are lovely, with memorable design quirks like vintage colored leather chairs, bedside lamps made from plumping pipes, and the coolest tile floors in the bathrooms. Be prepared, though, that rooms this reasonable come at the expense of a few amenities—there's no room service, and no mini bar. Not that you'd need one, though, as the food scene is unsurprisingly a huge part of the draw—The Decadente is one of Lisbon's coolest restaurants, and the rooftop bar, The Insólito, is perpetually full of locals grabbing post-work drinks.

Located in an ancient courtyard in the city’s historic area of Alfama, Memmo Alfama was one of the first boutique hotels in the area, and is still one of the best hotels in Lisbon. From the cozy living room check-in, to its forty-two rooms with amazing views, every inch of the place is intimate and relaxing. The terrace and pool, which also boast incredible views of the river and surrounding city, is the perfect spot for a glass of wine. Plus, the property is only minutes from downtown, and the famous yellow tram (a great way to explore the city) stops nearby, too.

56 Rua D. Pedro V, Príncipe Real

Hotelier Rodrigo Machaz's third property is set on the top of a hill in the decidedly cool Príncipe Real neighborhood, giving it both a full-circle view of the city (best viewed from the open-air patio of their rooftop bar) and incredible access to some of Lisbon's best shopping and restaurants. Machaz's style is laid back, intimate—only 41 rooms here—and experience-focused, but that doesn't mean his properties skimp on luxury. In addition to the stunning rooftop pool, the hotel is known for high-touch, attentive service, including a concierge with the best recommendations we've come across. Room décor is minimalist but textured, with fur throws at the foot of the bed, floor-to-ceiling paneled headboards, and sleek limestone bathrooms. Leave time for drinks and cocktails at the excellent on-site bar and restaurant.

Located on a hilltop in the Lapa District of Lisbon, this historic 19th-century palace-turned-hotel offers stunning views of the Tagus River just a short drive from central Lisbon. The hotel was completely renovated in 2003, yet retains much of the timeless charm it had when it was originally built 170 years ago. You can opt for views of the river, or the regal garden and pool; each room or suite features equally impressive décor that varies from Art Deco to colonial to neo-classic styling.

The One Palácio da Anunciada is one of those gorgeously decrepit sixteenth-century palaces that’s had a contemporary vibrancy breathed back into its hallways—while maintaining the integrity of its past. The grand blush marble staircase that sweeps up from the ornate lobby feels all of 400-plus years old, but the guest rooms belong to 2019. Big beds, bigger bathrooms, and Nespresso machines fill the cool, creamy interiors. The spa area is small but mighty with stellar massages and facials on offer alongside an indoor plunge pool and a steam room. High up at the hotel’s crown is the real reason you came here. The hotel’s outdoor pool seems to hover above the city—a rare indulgence in the capital. 70 Rua do Alecrim, Bairro Alto

Mon-Thurs: 12pm-12am

Fri-Sat: 12pm-2am

Entrepreneurs and brothers Duarte Cardoso Pinto and Gustavo and António Paulo Duarte bought Palácio Chiado in 2014, when the 18th-century palace sat in empty disrepair. Over the course of almost two years, they carefully restored the place, breathing new life into the gold-leaf chandeliers, elaborate frescoes and stucco work, and stained glass windows to make a home for their upscale food court program: A series of restaurants and bars spread out over the full two floors of the space. It's worth visiting for the building alone, but the food is deserving of the setting—we like Delisbon for exhaustively sourced charcuterie and cheese, and Local Chiado for locally sourced, veggie-forward quinoa bowls and sugar-free desserts. If you like fish, try Bacalhau Lisboa, a Portuguese spot that serves traditional iterations of codfish the same way it's been cooked here for generations. There's also a bar and a more formal restaurant for a sit-down dining experience.
