[Pap'Açôrda](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/papacorda)

49 Av. 24 de Julho, Bairro Alto

Tues-Wed, Sun: 12pm-12am

Thurs-Sat: 12pm-2am

Pap'Açôrda, an old Lisbon classic that's recently moved to a brand-new location in the Time Out Market, came highly recommended from several people we asked. Chef Manuela Brandão has been with the restaurant since they first opened in the '80s, and he's known for classic Portuguese dishes like arroz de cabidela, açordas, and a chocolate mousse that helped first make the restaurant famous. There space is huge and there are two long bars (plus an excellent wine and cocktail menu), so while it's worth making a reservation for a big night out, it's also a good place for last-minute cocktails and snacks.

[![Image 24: Petisqueira Matateu](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Petisqueira-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chueca/petisqueira)

[Petisqueira Matateu](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chueca/petisqueira)

Estádio do Restelo, Chueca

Tue-Thu: 7pm-11pm

Fri: 12:30pm-3pm, 7pm-11:30pm 

Sat: 12:30pm-4pm, 7pm-11:30pm 

Sun: 12:30pm-4pm, 7pm-11pm

This sweet little gastropub (inside Estadió do Restelo) is decorated like a design-conscious homage to its namesake, a famous Portuguese soccer player, with tables topped with lacquered newspaper articles, vintage framed jerseys, and original posters on the walls. The menu offers cheap Portuguese tapas and plenty of inexpensive beer, and while it's obviously a place to grab food before or during a game, it's also worth checking out at quieter times, when you can explore the stadium (which is built on an old quarry) without the crowds.

[![Image 25: Restaurante Magano](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/magano.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/o-magano)

[Restaurante Magano](https://goop.com/place/o-magano)

 R. Tomás da Anunciação 52A, Campo de Ourique

Restaurante Magano is a refined but still resolutely local spot (we were the only tourists in the place). Our chatty, intuitive server decided to skip the standard menu explanation and instead brought platters of what she figured we would like—cold seafood salad, bowls of chickpeas saturated in grassy green olive oil, and plenty of buttery rice. She guessed right. Pro tip: Reservations are essential, but make them late—no one eats before 8 p.m. in this town.

[![Image 26: Solar Dos Nunes](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/solar-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/solar-dos-nunes)

[Solar Dos Nunes](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/solar-dos-nunes)

68 Rua dos Lusiadas, Belém

This cozy, rustic little spot has occupied a corner in Belém for years, with the same décor—the walls are packed with framed, edge-to-edge positive reviews and write-ups stacked above blue-and-white tiles. The fresh, gorgeous seafood is a good bet order-wise, and each meal starts with appetizers that the waiter brings to your table automatically (a huge benefit when you're exhausted and starving from a day of sight-seeing).

[![Image 27: Solar Dos Presuntos](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Solar-dos-Presuntos-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/baixa/solar-dos-presuntos)

[Solar Dos Presuntos](https://goop.com/place/portugal/baixa/solar-dos-presuntos)

150 Rua Portas de Santo Antão, Baixa

This old-school, white tablecloth restaurant (which has been open in this space since the '70s), is our pick for classic Portuguese food and fresh-as-it-gets seafood, with an extensive wine list to match. Fish are purchased in the markets each morning, so it's best to opt for classic, lightly prepared foods like the grilled lobster tails with a squeeze of lemon or, for the brave, an incredible salt-crusted fish that the waiter presents and filets for you at the table. For littles, there's an endlessly entertaining lobster tank in the front of the restaurant.

[![Image 28: Topo](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Topo-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/topo)

[Topo](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/topo)

Commercial Center Martim Moniz, Chiado

Great views are a dime a dozen in a city this hilly, but the view from this rooftop bar on the top floor of a busy shopping center (which looks straight out over the castle) is one of the best by far. They're known for great brunch, excellent cocktails, and dignified, destination-worthy bar food, and on the weekends a DJ sets up shop in the corner for long nights in the open air. Sister restaurant Topo Chiado (which also occupies a rooftop) is worth checking out too.

[![Image 29: 100 Maneiras](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Maneiras-5.png)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/100-maneiras)

[100 Maneiras](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/100-maneiras)

39 Rua do Teixeira, Bairro Alto

Though he was actually born in Yugoslavia, and didn't move to Portugal until 1997, Ljubomir Stanisic has become one of the country's most well-known celebrity chefs—in addition to his restaurants and books, he's also a consulting chef for Six Senses in Europe and a host of the Portuguese version of Kitchen Nightmares. 100 Maneiras is his original restaurant, and it remains a Lisbon classic. With only 30 seats, it's incredibly intimate—an experience that's furthered by a remarkably well-priced tasting menu. The menu itself changes seasonally, save for one signature item: Stanisic's "codfish clothesline," which is exactly what it sounds like, yet surprisingly appealing.

[![Image 30: Clube de Fado](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/clube-de-fado_1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/clube-de-fado)

[Clube de Fado](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/clube-de-fado)

86–94 Rua S. João Praça, Alfama

This is a wonderful, aptly named late-night spot where you can get your dose of Fado; it's the kind of comfortable local place where you can end a night with a good meal, a gorgeous set of songs, and a glass of brandy.

[![Image 31: Lost In](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/LostIn1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/lost-in)

[Lost In](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/lost-in)

56 Rua Dom Pedro V, Príncipe Real

Mon: 4pm-12am

Tues-Sat: 12:30pm-12am

To get to this quirky terrace bar and café, you'll first navigate a maze-like Indian clothing store via the back door before being met with its stunning rooftop view. Comfortable outdoor seating, shaded by colorful umbrellas, makes for a tranquil environment perfect for an afternoon drink or a light meal.

[![Image 32: Lux Frágil](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/LuxFragil4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/lux-fragil)

[Lux Frágil](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/lux-fragil)

Av. Infante D. Henrique, Armazém A, Cais da Pedra a Sta Apolónia, Alfama

One of Portugal's most popular venues, Lux Frágil has remained a fixture of Lisbon nightlife since opening in 1998. Located near the waterfront, with three distinct but connected areas—a club, a bar, and a rooftop lounge—the interior is a sleek and fashionable setting for weekly events consisting of mostly house, techno, and disco music, presented by an impressive selection of well-known DJs. If you’re not a hardcore dancer, you can stick to the upstairs bar, which is a bit more laid back. Beware: As one of Lisbon’s most famous clubs, the line gets pretty long on the weekends, so it's best to arrive on the earlier side.

[Ministerium](https://goop.com/place/portugal/baixa/ministerium)

72 Praça do Comércio, Baixa

If you're up for a night of dancing, make your way to the Ministerium, where you'll find the perfect pairing of old and new Lisbon. The space, which once housed the Portuguese Ministry of Finance, was transformed a few years ago into a cantina by day and nighttime modern dance club, where 18th-century vaulted ceilings meet modern dance music (with some of the best techno-electronic DJs from Lisbon and around the world), all conveniently located near Lisbon’s largest square, the Praça do Comércio. Most dance spots in Lisbon don't get going until after midnight, and this one keeps going until 6am.

[Park Bar](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/park-bar)

58 Calçada do Combro, Bairro Alto

Park Bar was once a rooftop parking lot (and it's still perched on top of one), to which it owes its ample space and concrete floor, but little else: This sleek, hip spot is completely transformed with wood furniture, nice evening lighting, and—like many others of Lisbon's best—a great view of the Tagus River. While a drink with this view is enough of a reason to stop by, Park also has a steady rotation of live music, good DJs, and outdoor movie screenings.

[Pavilhão Chinês](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/pavilhao-chines)

V89 Rua Dom Pedro, Príncipe Real

Filled with small gadgets, figurines, and toys from the early twentieth century, this five-room bar is the perfect setting for a conversation over a drink or two. The vibe is super relaxed—not at all scene-y—with lots of comfortable seating. Even if you're not in the mood for a drink, it's worth it to at least go inside and take a peek at it unique décor.

[Pensão Amor](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/pensao-amor)

19 Rua do Alecrim, Bairro Alto

The name of this eclectic spot translates roughly into “Love House”, a reference to its provocative past: The intimate little bar was built inside an 18-century bordello. Elaborate décor reflects this heritage, with furniture upholstered in rich red velvet, frescos spread across the ceiling, and walls adorned with mirrors, vintage paintings, and posters of burlesque women. (The club also features live burlesque shows, in a room appropriately decorated in gold and leopard print.)

[![Image 37: Pharmacia](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Pharmacia2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/pharmacia)

[Pharmacia](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/pharmacia)

1 Rua de Santa Catarina, Bairro Alto

In the same building as the Pharmacy Museum, the owners of Pharmacia went long on their theme. The walls here are lined with medicine cabinets, each filled with antique pill bottles, vials, and boxes of medication. The food (a classically Portuguese menu) is perfectly good, but we really come here for the cocktails, named for prescriptions (Ibuprofen, Morphine, LSD) and served in beakers. Anything on ice is brought to the table in a first-aid-kit-turned-ice-bucket, and water is served in an Erlenmeyer flask. Ask for a seat on patio, which is flanked by old, pastel-pink buildings and looks out over the water.

[![Image 38: Pub Lisboeta](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/PubLisboeta1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/pub-lisboeta)

[Pub Lisboeta](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/pub-lisboeta)

63 Rua Dom Pedro V, Príncipe Real

This laid-back bar occupies a tiny space that's made to feel more spacious with the liberal use of mirrors on each wall and emerald subway tiling that approximates a wainscoting along the walls and the bar. During the week when it's a little sleepy in here, set up at one of the bar chairs or one of a few small tables in the front for bar snacks, sandwiches, and a menu that shows the breadth of Portugal's growing craft beer movement. On Friday and Saturday nights, the space fills up with locals, who you'll find lingering out in the street when the bar itself gets too crowded.

[Botequim](https://goop.com/place/portugal/graca/botequim-da-graca)

79 Largo Graça, Graça

First opened in the late '60s by Portuguese writer Natália Correia—and then closed after her death—Botequim re-opened in 2010: a quirky bar/café serving food, wine, and cocktails to locals through the late evening. Portions are hearty, and you can expect items like prago, a baked steak sandwich in cream mustard sauce, on the menu; the space often hosts music and poetry gatherings, so don’t be surprised if you stumble into one in the evening.

[![Image 40: Conserveira de Lisboa](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/ConserveiradeLisboa2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/conserveira-de-lisboa)

[Conserveira de Lisboa](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/conserveira-de-lisboa)

34 Rua dos Bacalhoeiros, Alfama

Opened in the 1930's and virtually unchanged ever since, Conserveira de Lisboa (Lisbon Cannery), sells mainly brightly colored vintage tins of fish. Quirky as it is, its charm is undeniable, whatever your culinary proclivities may be.

[Copenhagen Coffee Lab](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/copenhagen-coffee-lab)

10 Rua Nova da Piedade, Príncipe Real

Mon-Fri: 8am-7pm

Sat-Sun: 9:30am-7pm

With its white stools, white walls, and decidedly minimalist interiors, this coffee shop is what you might expect from Danish owners. Pleasant and unassuming, you’ll find some serious coffee nerds behind the bar, where you can get your fix by V60, Chemex, aeropress, or French press. Good music, decadent cake, various pastries, and a nearby outdoor square make this a great stop—whether you’re in it for the excellent coffee, or not.

[![Image 42: Darwin's Café](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/DarwinCafe1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/darwins-cafe)

[Darwin's Café](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/darwins-cafe)

Av. Brasília, Ala B, Belém

Mon: 12:30pm-4pm

Tues-Sun: 12:30pm-3:30pm, 4:30pm-6:30pm, 7:30pm-11pm

As a part of the Champalimaud Foundation’s medical science research center, Darwin’s Café shares the fabulous architecture and waterfront views of their new building. Mod leather seating, floor-to-ceiling windows, and cool artwork (inspired by Charles Darwin's original drawings) look out onto the terrace, which takes full advantage of the location and panoramic scene. The food is great, too—be sure to try one of their inventive risottos.

[![Image 43: Hello, Kristof](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/HelloKristof2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/hello-kristof)

[Hello, Kristof](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/hello-kristof)

103 Rua do Poço dos Negros, Bairro Alto

Opened by a freelance graphic designer who felt too isolated doing work from home, this welcoming café is the perfect place to set up shop for the afternoon with a laptop or a book. Quality coffee, fresh pastries, and a wall of independent magazines all contribute to its cozy, comfortable vibes.

[![Image 44: Manteigaria](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Manteirgaria.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/manteigaria)

[Manteigaria](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/manteigaria)

Rua do Loreto 2, Bairro Alto

Watching Manteigaria’s bakers expertly knock out hundreds (if not thousands) of those sweet, blistered custard tarts in minutes is, to say the least, captivating. Fuel up with thimbles of the bakery’s velvety espresso and one or two still-warm tarts dusted in cinnamon sugar.

[The Mill](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/the-mill-2)

1 Rua do Poço dos Negros, Bairro Alto

Mon-Fri: 8am-6pm 

Sat-Sun: 9am-5pm

The owners of this cozy modern café are Portuguese and Australian—and you can count on The Mill both for a great wine list, which rotates every few months, and also healthy breakfast fare like bircher muesli and avocado toast with poached eggs. The menu is designed around seasonal produce—and you can always stop by for fresh bagels, pastries, and excellent coffee. The staff is warm and helpful; it’s the kind of place you could stop in for a quick breakfast, or easily kill an entire afternoon.

[![Image 46: Pastéis de Belém](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/pasteisdebelem1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/pasteis-de-belem)

[Pastéis de Belém](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/pasteis-de-belem)

84-92 Rua Belém, Belém

No trip to Lisbon would be complete without a visit to its world-renowned confectionary shop, the Pastéis de Belem. The bakery serves delicate custard-filled tarts (pastel de nata) with a storied history: The recipe—conceived by the monks of Jeronimo's Monastery in 1837, and unchanged to this day—remains a carefully guarded secret, passed down from generation to generation, so you won't find them anywhere else. There may be a line, but it’s worth the wait—don’t forget to top it off with cinnamon and powdered sugar.

[![Image 47: Piriquita Café](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/casa-piriquita-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/sintra/piriquita-cafe)

[Piriquita Café](https://goop.com/place/portugal/sintra/piriquita-cafe)

1/18 Rua das Padarias, Sintra

Not exactly a well-kept secret, this wonderful bakery was founded in Sintra in 1862, and has been known for its pastries ever since. Come for the queijadas, small, crispy pies filled with cheese, sugar, and a little cinnamon, and travesseiros, the famous pillow-like cake (made with egg cream, almond, and other amazing stuff) that was invented here.

[![Image 48: Silva & Feijoo](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/SilvaFeijoo1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/silva-feijoo)

[Silva & Feijoo](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/silva-feijoo)

117 Rua dos Bacalhoeiros, Alfama

This legendary kitchen and gourmet shop is worth visiting for the facade alone—practically untouched since the store opened almost a hundred years ago, it features ornate, gold-painted signage and old-school merchandising windows. The shelves are filled with Portuguese products like cans of sardines and tuna, homemade jams and quinces, oils, wine, spirits, and crackers. It's an ideal place to pick up souvenirs.

[![Image 49: Sol e Pesca](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/SolePesca1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/sol-e-pesca)

[Sol e Pesca](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/sol-e-pesca)

44 Rua Nova do Carvalho, Bairro Alto

Mon-Thurs: 12pm-2am

Fri-Sat: 12pm-4am

This place is all about preserved seafood. While you could have a full meal here with table service, the best way to experience it is to choose a couple of cans of fish, and order some bread and wine to accompany. It's also a great place to stop in for picnic supplies (they have a counter for quick grab-and-go orders).

[![Image 50: Time Out Market](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/TimeOut2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/time-out-market)

[Time Out Market](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/time-out-market)

49 Av. 24 de Julho, Bairro Alto

Mon-Thurs: 10am-12am

Fri-Sat: 10am-2am

Sun: 10am-12am

This renovated market, part of Mercado da Ribeira, Lisbon's biggest fresh food market, has all the trappings of your typical food court—picnic-style community tables, food stalls, and large crowds—except the food itself is exceptional. It's a way to try a variety of dishes from a bunch of different top Portuguese chefs at once; there are thirty-five kiosks, with a not-to-be-missed spot from Henrique Sá Pessoa of Alma among them. Plus, there's ample outdoor seating on their adjacent terraces.

[![Image 51: A Vida Portuguesa](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/A-Vida-Portuguesa-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/a-vida-portuguesa)

[A Vida Portuguesa](https://goop.com/place/portugal/chiado/a-vida-portuguesa)

72 R. Nova do Almada, Chiado

This shop sells mostly classic Portuguese products—from kitchenware to toiletries, to stationery, to... detergent and floor wax (in colorful and graphic old-school packaging, of course). It’s the perfect spot to find a gift or a souvenir, and their gift boxes (random assortments of perfectly kitsch products) are hard to resist.

[![Image 52: Embaixada](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Embaixada4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/embaixada)

[Embaixada](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/embaixada)

26 Praça do Príncipe Real, Príncipe Real

One of Lisbon's most impressive developments, Embaixada is a series of shops that form a gallery inside a neo-Moorish palace. All of the vendors are local, so the entire shopping experience feels like a celebration of Portuguese design and craftsmanship. The range of shops is huge—come here for everything from swimsuits to antique clothing to gifts and accessories.

[![Image 53: Fashion Clinic](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/FashionClinic1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenida-de-la-libertad/fashion-clinic)

[Fashion Clinic](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenida-de-la-libertad/fashion-clinic)

144 Av. Liberdade, Avenida de la Libertad

Mon-Sat: 10am-8pm

Sun: 10am-7pm

One of Portugal's only department stores, Fashion Clinic has floor space devoted to all the major designers (Stella McCartney, Isabel Marant, Prada, etc.), making it an indispensable part of Lisbon's fashion scene, if not necessarily known for showcasing Portuguese designers. Though the store has been in existence since the '90s, it got a major revitalization when it was purchased by Portuguese businesswoman Paula Amorim in 2005. Leave some time to check out the well-curated lifestyle section, which stocks everything from Diptyque candles to Smythson notebooks.

[![Image 54: Feira Da Ladra](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/fiera-da-ladra-1.jpeg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/graca/feira-da-ladra)

[Feira Da Ladra](https://goop.com/place/portugal/graca/feira-da-ladra)

Campo de Santa Clara, Graça

Tue: 6am-5pm

Sat: 6am-5pm

Lisbon's big open air flea market, which has been taking place since the 12th century, now assembles every Tuesday and Sunday. It's admittedly a bit all-over-the-place, so finding the good stuff can take some hunting, but if you're patient, you can find furniture, old postcards, antiques, and vintage clothes and accessories. Fiera da Ladra translates roughly to "thief fair," which is to say that haggling is central to the experience. Photos: Marco Verch

[![Image 55: Loja Real](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/LojaReal5.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/loja-real)

[Loja Real](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/loja-real)

20 Praça do Príncipe Real, Príncipe Real

This adorable shop in Príncipe Real is a go-to for European (and often handmade) kids' brands, featuring everything from beautifully painted wooden blocks, to sleekly designed teething toys, to the teeniest little espadrilles. The buyers also have a few beachy homewares around for mom—baskets, oversized totes, and Turkish towels are scattered throughout the space.

[![Image 56: Solar Antiques](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/solar1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/solar)

[Solar Antiques](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/solar)

70 Rua Dom Pedro V, Príncipe Real

Mon-Fri: 10am-7pm

Sat: 10am-1pm

This shop is decorated from floor to ceiling in stunning, intricate, and mostly blue-and-white antique tiles from every era of Portuguese history. Collectors who know what they're looking for will have a field day here, but it's just as pleasurable an outing for naive tourists (some small tiles come in at a price range that's reasonable enough for a souvenir).

[![Image 57: Cinemateca Portuguesa](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Cinematica2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/cinemateca-portuguesa)

[Cinemateca Portuguesa](https://goop.com/place/portugal/principe-real/cinemateca-portuguesa)

39 Rua Barata Salgueiro, Príncipe Real

Part film archive, part museum, and part movie theater, Cinemateca Portuguesa is the kind of place where you can wander in and watch an Ernst Lubitsch silent film accompanied by live piano. They screen a variety of classics; and there's a convenient restaurant and quiet patio in the back, too.

[![Image 58: Day Trip to Cascais](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/cascais-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/cascais/day-trip-to-cascais)

[Day Trip to Cascais](https://goop.com/place/portugal/cascais/day-trip-to-cascais)

This picturesque little village is a short drive from Lisbon and has some really great beaches, so it makes for a good day trip if you'd like to spend some time by the ocean sunbathing, surfing, or SUP. There's fascinating history in Cascais, too; originally a sleepy fishing village, it became a glitzy getaway for the Portuguese royal family in the late 19th century, and was famously the home of the Spanish King when he was exiled during the Franco regime. Cascais feels very much like a resort today, and accordingly, there are a few incredible hotels: Albatroz, Villa Cascais, and Oitavos all make excellent options if you'd like to make a weekend out of it. Photos: g.sighele

[![Image 59: Day Trip to Sintra](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/sintra-2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/sintra/day-trip-to-sintra)

[Day Trip to Sintra](https://goop.com/place/portugal/sintra/day-trip-to-sintra)

The hill town of Sintra stays a little cooler than the city in the summer months, so it's been royal vacation destination for centuries—and has the castles to prove it. The Pena Palace (which has a German vibe, architecturally) gets a lot of attention for its bright pink and yellow exterior and hilltop location, but it's worth going inside, as the interior is equally (if not more) dramatic. It's also worth buying a ticket to the National Palace—style-wise it's a hodgepodge, since it was inhabited by so many different royals over the years, but the intricate tile work on the walls is like nothing else. Sintra is only a forty-minute drive from Lisbon, so it's an easy day trip, but there are more than a few hotels that are worth checking out if you want to spend the night. Lawrence's Hotel is a darling bed and breakfast with incredible views from each room, and Tivoli Palacio is a full-fledged palace that's been renovated into a luxury hotel, complete with a dream-worthy pool deck. Whether you come for the day or make a weekend out of it, we recommend buying the bus pass that takes you around to each castle—it's a hop-on-hop-off shuttle that makes the entire experience incredibly easy. Photos: Daniel GB

[![Image 60: Explore Alfama](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/alfama-1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/explore-alfama)

[Explore Alfama](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alfama/explore-alfama)

Alfama

Alfama is one of Portugal's oldest districts, and since the hilly area is filled with sets of stairs and narrow alleys, it's best explored by foot (though the 1930's-style tram that makes up the only public transportation here is worth hopping on for fun). The neighborhood's never really been tony, and though younger generations have taken over several restaurants and storefronts, the original community is still very much intact thanks to generous rent control programs. There are several attractions worth exploring while you're here. Start with Castelo de São Jorge, the beautifully restored site of the Christians' 12th-century defeat of the Moors, where there are tons of lookouts with views of the sea and surrounding neighborhoods. Also visit the Church of St. Anthony, the birthplace of its namesake, the patron saint of lovers—newly married couples often leave flowers here in hopes of a happy marriage, and single people try to throw coins into his book for good luck finding a partner. Though it's not a must, it's fun to check out the Fado Museum, which memorializes a specific musical style born in Alfama: a solemn, dramatic singing and guitar style originally sung by the wives of sailors at sea. Photos: Dirk Olberz

[![Image 61: Galeria Zé dos Bois](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/ZeDosBois1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/galeria-ze-dos-bois)

[Galeria Zé dos Bois](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/galeria-ze-dos-bois)

59 Rua da Barroca, Bairro Alto

This teensy room (which opens up onto a lovely outdoor terrace) hosts experimental performance art and musical acts, plus a sprinkling of dance and theatre, both by local musicians and international creatives that the organization brings in. It's an excellent place to get a sense for the local creative scene, and makes an equally nice night-out activity.

[![Image 62: Boost Portugal](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/GoCar1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/baixa/gocar-2)

[Boost Portugal](https://goop.com/place/portugal/baixa/gocar-2)

16 Rua dos Douradores, Baixa

Leaning into being a tourist (or playing tourist in your own city for a day) can be extremely entertaining. Such is the case with Boost Portugal's cool take on the common city tour: a talking, GPS-guided go-cart vehicle that takes you around the big—as well as some lesser known—sights of Lisbon. Following the suggested routes laid out for you is simple, as is making an unplanned pit stop for photos, or veering off to do more of your own thing. Each car fits two people (the driver must be at least twenty-one years old, but kids can ride shotgun); small groups and families can reserve a mini fleet of their own.

[![Image 63: Jardim da Estrela](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/JardimdaEstrela-Andrea-mann-Flickr.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/estrela/jardim-da-estrela)

[Jardim da Estrela](https://goop.com/place/portugal/estrela/jardim-da-estrela)

1200-667 Praça da Estrela, Estrela

Nestled into a sweet neighborhood on top of a hill and directly across from Estrela Basilica, this low-key park is a great place to take littles or go for a walk. The original design was a formal English garden, so you'll find interesting varietals, a pond, and an ornate green gazebo near the middle. Photo: Andrea Mann

[![Image 64: LX Factory](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/LXFactory6.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alcantara/lx-factory)

[LX Factory](https://goop.com/place/portugal/alcantara/lx-factory)

103 Rua Rodrigues de Faria, Alcantara

This creative mini-neighborhood, where you can wander through restaurants, cafes, shops, and design studios occupies a heavily graffiti-ed industrial site. A hangout and workspace for members of Lisbon's vibrant creative crowd, it's also a nice repose from the more touristic parts of town. The Ler Devagar bookstore, which makes up the central hub of the development, is built around a two-story printing press and features floor-to-ceiling shelves of books.

[![Image 65: Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/M-SAO-PEDRO-DE-ALCANTARA_2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/miradouro-de-sao-pedro-de-alcantara)

[Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara](https://goop.com/place/portugal/bairro-alto/miradouro-de-sao-pedro-de-alcantara)

Rua São Pedro de Alcântara, Bairro Alto

Of course, Lisbon has no shortage of great views, but this is one of the best: Here, you'll find a panoramic look at the city from a scenic perch with a fountain and gardens. Plus, it's right next to the Elevador da Glória, the city's little yellow tram, which can take you from Bairro Alto to the center of the city.

[![Image 66: Mosteiro dos Jerónimos](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/JeronimosMonastery-Flickr-Paulo-Valdivieso-.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/mosteiro-dos-jeronimos)

[Mosteiro dos Jerónimos](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/mosteiro-dos-jeronimos)

Praça do Império, Belém

Secular since the 1800's, Jerónimos Monastery is designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of the incredible Manueline-style architecture, all done in limestone over the course of more than one hundred years. It's a required tourist destination because it's so photogenic (sculptures and intricate design elements are carved into every detail), but the grounds are enormous, so particularly if you come by on a weekday, you'll have plenty of moments to yourself. Photos: Paulo Valdivieso, Shadowgate

[![Image 67: Museu Berardo](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/BerardoCollection1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/museu-berardo)

[Museu Berardo](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/museu-berardo)

Praça do Império, Belém

Halfway between the Tower of Belém and Jerónimo's Monastery in the heart of the city's Belém District, this museum houses the collection of Lisbon businessman José Manuel Rodrigues Berardo, with a particular emphasis on Portugal's finest contemporary artists. The permanent collection contains the works of Pablo Picasso, Salvador Dalí, Marcel Duchamp, and Andy Warhol (which are always on view on the second floor), but they also organize rotating, temporary exhibitions that bring in works outside the collection. There's a lot for kids to enjoy, and admission is free.

[![Image 68: Museu Calouste Gulbenkian](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/gulbenkian-4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenidas-novas/museu-calouste-gulbenkian)

[Museu Calouste Gulbenkian](https://goop.com/place/portugal/avenidas-novas/museu-calouste-gulbenkian)

45A Av. de Berna, Avenidas Novas

Calouste Gulbenkian was actually a British collector, but he lived a very international life, growing up in Turkey and traveling extensively during his career. In that context, it's not so surprising that his collection is housed in Lisbon, where he spent his final years. One of the largest in Europe, it claims significant holdings of Egyptian and Greco-Roman art, Armenian art, and impressionists like Manet, Degas, and Monet. There's also an impressive contemporary collection, built with funds from Gulbenkian's foundation, which was created with his fortune after his death. Exhibitions switch over frequently, and there's always a great mix of old and new on the walls, so it's entirely worthy of repeat visits.

[![Image 69: Museu de Arte, Arquitetura e Tecnologia](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/MAAT3.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/museu-de-arte-arquitetura-e-tecnologia)

[Museu de Arte, Arquitetura e Tecnologia](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/museu-de-arte-arquitetura-e-tecnologia)

Av. Brasília, Belém

Situated right along the riverfront, the Museum of Art, Architecture, and Technology (MAAT) is one of the most recent additions to Lisbon's historic Belém District. Designed by the British architect Amanda Levete, the oval-shaped building is strikingly modern, allowing for individuals to walk along the top and take in the views; the new structure sits beside the Tejo Power Station, an older building that exemplifies Portuguese industrial architecture from the beginning of the 20th century and has housed a museum of electricity for many years. The schedule at MAAT is refreshingly eclectic, offering both standard contemporary art exhibitions and hybrid presentations that explore everything from music to performance art to the history (and future) of technology. Suitable for all ages.

[![Image 70: Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Museu-Nacional-de-Arte-Antiga1.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/museu-nacional-de-arte-antiga)

[Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga](https://goop.com/place/portugal/lapa/museu-nacional-de-arte-antiga)

Rua das Janelas Verdes, Lapa

Opened in 1884, the National Museum of Ancient Art contains the largest collection of public art in Lisbon. Hailing from Portugal and around the world, the artwork varies from sculpture and painting to decorative arts, covering a range of periods from the Middle Ages to present. Leave time to lounge on the outdoor terrace afterwards.

[![Image 71: Museo Nacional do Azulejo](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Museu-Nacional-do-Azulejo4.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/penha-de-franca/museo-nacional-do-azulejo)

[Museo Nacional do Azulejo](https://goop.com/place/portugal/penha-de-franca/museo-nacional-do-azulejo)

4 Rua Madre Deus , Penha de França

What Guinness is to Ireland, tiles are to Portugal, so it goes without saying that the National Tile Museum is a must-see: Housed in a 16th century convent, it features a collection of tiles that spans centuries, from the Renaissance through present day.

[![Image 72: Museu Nacional dos Coches](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/MuseuNacionalDosCoches2.jpg)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/museu-nacional-dos-coches)

[Museu Nacional dos Coches](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/museu-nacional-dos-coches)

136 Av. da Índia, Belém

Locals weren't universally pleased when the long-standing Coach Museum moved from its beloved location in an 18th-century riding arena to a sleek, modern new building across the street in recent years. Though the new building brought much-needed space for the impressive collection, many worried that the stark surroundings served to sterilize the opulent gilded carriages on display. Despite the (ongoing) debate over the architecture, it's a mistake to skip this unique museum, devoted to transportation before cars. Inside, you'll find incredible carriages, cabriolets, and even some sedan chairs that housed Portuguese royalty dating back to the 1600's. Die-hards can visit the old riding arena across the street, which still houses a small collection.

[![Image 73: Torre de Belém](https://goop-img.com/cdn-cgi/image/height=75,width=100,fit=crop,gravity=0.5x0.5,quality=95,format=auto,onerror=redirect,metadata=copyright/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/belemtower1.png)](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/torre-de-belem)

[Torre de Belém](https://goop.com/place/portugal/belem/torre-de-belem)

Av. Brasília, Belém

This 16th-century tower, one of the city's most iconic landmarks, sits along the Tagus river. While the four-story structure was originally built to defend the capital against invaders, it has also welcomed Portuguese sailors home since the age of the great explorers; now, you can wander through its sparse inner chambers (littles, especially, will have fun exploring) and drink in the stunning Moorish architecture.

Conquer ancient Moorish walls with spectacular views over Sintra.

### The Moorish Castle Tickets

[**Castle of the Moors: Entry Ticket + Optional Audio Guide**](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-p975020/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tf_p975020)

If you’re visiting just the castle, the basic entry ticket gets you into the Moorish Castle with an optional audio guide. You’ll have plenty of time to explore the ancient walls and soak in those famous panoramic views over Sintra and the Atlantic coast.

[**Castle of the Moors: Skip The Line Ticket & Guided Tour**](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-skip-the-line-and-guided-tour-p1096623/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tf_p1096623)

The guided tour includes a one-hour walk with an English or Portuguese-speaking guide. It’s only €3.80 more than the basic ticket, and you’ll learn about the castle’s history from the Moorish period through to its 19th-century restoration. The guides know the best photo spots too.

[**🏰 Sintra Combo: Pena Palace, Moorish Castle, Quinta da Regaleira**](https://www.getyourguide.com/lisbon-l42/lisbon-sintra-tour-to-pena-palace-castle-and-regaleira-t551556/?partner_id=FENKESD&utm_medium=online_publisher&cmp=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tf_t551556)

Many visitors combine the Moorish Castle with Pena Palace, Quinta da Regaleira, and Sintra town. The private BMW tour (€325 per person, 8 hours) handles all the logistics – transportation between sites, skip-the-line access, and a guide who knows the area inside out. It’s pricier, but when you factor in transport costs and time saved, it makes sense for a special trip.

![Image 2: View of the Moorish Castle walls in Sintra.](https://cdn.shortpixel.ai/spai/q_lossy+w_726+to_auto+ret_img/www.lisboacard.org/wp-content/uploads/moorish-castle-sintra-overlook-1758169638.jpg)cellar-door/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/sintra-portugal-may-2016-castle-moors-sintra-portugal-241995458.html)

*   Stroll along crumbling medieval ramparts as you trace Sintra’s history stone by stone.
*   Soak in bird’s-eye views of Sintra’s other major landmarks – Pena Palace, Quinta de Regaleira Estate, and lush Sintra forests – from the castle’s high vantage points.
*   Skip the ticket line and head straight to the walls when you pre-book online, giving you more time to explore.

## Tickets & Prices

Sintra’s Moorish Castle has two types of visits you can pre-book: self-guided and expert-led.

**[Self-guided Moorish Castle tickets](https://www.tiqets.com/en/sintra-attractions-c76496/tickets-for-castle-of-the-moors-skip-the-line-and-guided-tour-p1096623/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tl_p1096623-1)** let visitors move at their own pace, stopping to take in the medieval setting or the sweeping views of Sintra as long and as often as they want. There’s even a free Zoomguide audio app that will tell you about different parts of the castle as you come to them.

## Plan Your Visit

### Opening Hours

| Day | Opening Hours | Last Entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday – Sunday | 9:30 – 18:00 | 17:30 |

Last ticket and last admission at 17:30. Hours are often extended until 20:00 during Summer months, but make sure to verify in advance if you’re planning to go later.

The best time of day to visit the castle is right at opening time. The morning has the coolest weather in Sintra all year round, and, unlike other landmarks in Sintra, The Moorish Castle does not have many trees and shelters that will shade you from the sun during your trip.

### Getting There

From Lisbon, the easiest way to reach Sintra is by train on the **Sintra Line (CP)**, which departs every 30 minutes until 23:00 from Rossio, Oriente, or Entrecampos stations. The journey takes around 40 minutes.

Once at Sintra Station, you have a few options to reach The Moorish Castle:

Method Travel Time (incl. waits)Directions Notes
Taxi 15 mins Taxis are waiting in front of the station; ask one to take you to The Moorish Castle entrance.Fast and convenient; pricier than other options, especially in peak season.
Bus 25-40 mins Board the 434 “Circuito da Pena” bus and get off at The Moorish Castle stop Affordable and leaves every 15 mins; can be crowded in summer, sometimes with long queues.
Walking 50-65 mins uphill From the station, follow signs via historic center and forested paths to castle Free and scenic wooded path; steep climb, best for fit visitors who enjoy hiking.

### Map & Address (Location)

#### Castelo dos Mauros

![Image 3: Map of Castelo dos Mauros](blob:http://localhost/308dba39ab209b92ded169796cce9f4a)

2710-405 Sintra, Portugal · [Google Maps](https://maps.google.com/?q=38.792556,-9.3893376)

### Accessibility

The Moorish Castle is great for visitors with mobility issues for a few reasons:

*   A few handicap parking spaces are located near the entrance.
*   It is also the only one of Sintra’s major landmarks that allows dogs.
*   Manual wheelchairs are available at the ticket office. Visitors can rent one for free for 90 minutes of use.
*   Almost all areas of the castle are wheelchair-accessible. Most of the stone stairways are fitted with ramps or wheelchair lifts, and the castle walls are reachable by elevator. Maps at the ticketing office suggest a specific route to take through the castle to fully utilize the amenities.
*   Lots of the surfaces on the grounds are steep or uneven, but the ticketing desk loans out traction equipment that wheelchair users can employ to navigate the difficult terrain.
*   The gift shop, cafe, and restrooms at The Moorish Castle are also wheelchair-accessible.

### Etiquette

*   Stay on marked paths and ramparts – the parts of the castle that have not been reinforced are fragile.
*   Keep noise down at viewpoints – don’t disturb the castle’s serenity.
*   Respect the ruins – don’t touch or sit on fragile walls.
*   Be patient at bottlenecks – the walls only fit one-way traffic in spots; wait your turn instead of forcing past.
*   Secure your belongings – the walls can get seriously windy; secure hats, scarves, and even phones so they don’t fly off the ramparts.

## What to See & Do

### **Second Ring of Walls**

![Image 4: Tourists at the Moorish Castle in Sintra.](blob:http://localhost/de9d42c096e8a73885db044a60976344)
Even more than anywhere else in The Moorish Castle, strolling along the outer walls feels like walking through a medieval fantasy tale. The walls are rough and uneven, with ferns and ivy spilling through cracks.

### **Silos**

Peer inside these round pits in the ground and you’ll see smooth, cylindrical hollows carved into the rock and furnished with ancient-looking stone containers and tools. The silos are cool and shadowy, reminders of how supplies were once tucked safely below the earth.

### **Church of São Pedro de Canaferrim**

![Image 5: Church of São Pedro de Canaferrim, a small stone church with a wooden upper facade, nestled among trees at the Moorish Castle in Sintra.](blob:http://localhost/d4fd010b1ce0bc50b9ccecdc96e0e095) BY-SA 4.0 InternationalGualdimG/[Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Igreja_de_S%C3%A3o_Pedro_de_Canaferrim_12.jpg)

You’ll step from the wind and brightness of the ramparts and through a sturdy stone archway into a hushed, sheltered interior at this small church. Neither the exterior nor interior is lavish, but it feels like a sanctuary in the center of the busy castle; the air is cool, dim, and still, with a few panels explaining the church’s history.

### **Tomb & Christian Medieval Necropolis**

Even more so than the adjacent Church, the air in the Tomb & Christian Necropolis feels _thick_ and _humid_. The main reason is that the inside area is full of soil and greenery that add more moisture to the surroundings.

The graves and accompanying markers are simple—no towering crosses or ornate tombs, just faint outlines in the earth and the occasional small stone. They add a solemn layer to the visit, a reminder that the site once became not just a refuge, but a final resting place.

### **Arms Square**

![Image 6: Tourists at a stone tower of the Moorish Castle in Sintra, with flags of Portugal and Saudi Arabia flying nearby.](blob:http://localhost/ee9cd45a10f0141c3e44ad11af23b9e0)sepavone/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/moorish-castle-of-sintra-56136085.html)

The Royal Tower was a favorite retreat of King Ferdinand II.

This square in the center of the castle is a welcome open space after all the narrow stairways and passages. The floor is rough, gravelly, and open to the sky, and often filled with other visitors taking a break. The square was where people once gathered for safety during attacks on the areas around the castle, and now it’s the castle’s natural pause point.

### **Door of Betrayal**

The Door of Betrayal was built into the least-used part of the castle ramparts as a last resort escape hatch to the outside. It’s an unassuming black wooden gate that a lot of visitors miss, but knowing the heavy history behind it makes it an exciting landmark.

### **Towers & Viewpoints**

![Image 7: Stone battlement at the Moorish Castle in Sintra.](blob:http://localhost/b107239b864b80028f0fcdbbd58e60ae)andreslebedev/[Depositphotos](https://depositphotos.com/photo/medieval-castle-castelo-dos-mouros-sesimbra-portugal-48543493.html)

The steps to many of the castle’s towers and highest viewpoints are steep, uneven, and wind-exposed, but reaching the top rewards you with enormous panoramas. Some of the best viewpoints include:

**Viewpoint Name****Height Above Sea Level****What You Can See**
**Royal Tower**412 m / 1352 ft Wide-angle views of Pena Palace; Lisbon on clear days.
**Castle Keep**400 m / 1312 ft The best perspective of the castle itself, looking down over the Arms Square and inner walls.
**Northern Battlements**395 m / 1296 ft The rolling green valleys of Sintra.
**Western Ramparts**390 m / 1280 ft The Atlantic coast, with Cabo da Roca Cape visible in the distance.

## Did You Know That? Facts

1.   Features like the Cistern or the Arms Square were meant to serve as places for people to hide during attacks. Sintra was lucky enough to have a peaceful history, though, so the castle never served its defensive purpose.
2.   Centuries ago, the castle was surrounded by an Islamic settlement. Today, the settlement is gone and The Moorish Castle is one of the rare European castles that is just “stranded” on top of a hill with no town surrounding it.
3.   The Moorish Castle once functioned like a little city, with its own Islamic quarter, Christian church, necropolis, and more all crammed inside the fortress walls.

## Insider Tips

1.   Turn left when you enter – Most visitors instinctively head right and follow the battlements clockwise. If you go left instead, you’ll often find fewer people on the walls and get clearer photo angles.
2.   Catch the morning mist – Arrive early and you might see the castle floating above low-lying fog – an incredible sight.
3.   Pack a light layer, even in summer – The altitude means it’s often cooler and windier here than in central Sintra all year round.

## History (Timeline)

**700s-800s**

Built by the Moors to guard Sintra’s strategic mountain pass and to watch Lisbon’s approaches. Was never actually used.

**1100s-1200s**

Gradually loses military importance as Sintra’s population shifts downhill; parts of the castle fall into disuse.

**1300s-1400s**

Earthquakes and neglect leave the structure partially ruined and entirely abandoned.

**1755**

The Great Lisbon Earthquake causes extensive damage, reducing much of the fortress to rubble.

****1800s****

King Ferdinand II oversees partial restoration, reshaping the ruins into a Romantic-era monument alongside nearby Pena Palace.

******1995******

Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

## FAQs

### Do I need to book in advance?

Not required, but [booking online](https://www.tiqets.com/en/castelo-dos-mouros-sintra-tickets-l146205/?partner=lisboacard&tq_campaign=clis-en_tickets--castle-of-the-moors_mc_tl_l146205) saves time at the gate and locks in entry on busy days.

### Can I visit Pena Palace and the Moorish Castle on the same day?

Easily. They sit a short ride apart and pair well in one trip. Book [Pena ahead](https://www.lisboacard.org/tickets/pena-palace-park/), since its timed slots fill fast.

### Is the Moorish Castle covered by the Lisboa Card?

The [Lisboa Card](https://www.lisboacard.org/) gets you 15% off your ticket, and the train to Sintra is free.

### How long should I spend there?

About 1 to 1.5 hours for the walls, towers, and viewpoints. Photographers and hikers tend to stay longer.

São Jorge CastleIt is one of the ancient buildings in Lisbon and a major historical monument and tourist attraction in Lisbon. The castle is built onAlfamaThe high point of the area was a fortress when the Moors occupied Lisbon in the Middle Ages. Located on a commanding hillside, its presence can be seen from almost every corner of Lisbon. The castle originally belonged to the earlier Visigoths. After the Moorish invasion, it underwent large-scale expansion, and its walls, up to 8 m thick, still impress with their grandeur today. Here, people can better appreciate the city's architectural art, whether fromAlfamaTo the futuristic castles and drawbridges in the distant city, or in the urbanCarmo churchThe open-air ruins can be seen at a glance. National monument The architectural complex known as Lisbon castle and Lisbon city walls was classified as a national monument under the decree issued on June 16, 1910. The monument is owned by the Portuguese state and was temporarily transferred to Lisbon city hall on September 13, 1934, with the complete transfer finalized on May 31, 1942. On June 8, 1979, the revised terms of transfer for São Jorge Castle were officially enacted. Following the resolution of the Lisbon municipal council in October 1995, São Jorge Castle was placed under the management of the municipal company Empresa de Bairros Históricos de Lisboa (EBAHL). In 2003, this management responsibility was transferred to the municipal company Empresa de Gestão de Equipamentos e Animação Cultural (EGEAC). The site consists of a castle, the ruins of the Alcázar palace, the Plaza de Armas, a spacious viewing platform overlooking the entire city, a museum exhibition area, an archaeological exhibition area, several garden areas, and the city walls. The monument covers an area of approx. 4 hectares, surrounded by a massive perimeter wall and city walls, with one section of the wall coinciding with part of the boundary of Lisbon's old castle. Space and view In the past, there were no trees inside or outside the city walls; even if there were, the quantity was far less than today. In the days when the castle was merely a fortress to be conquered, it was absolutely unacceptable to provide the enemy with any tools for climbing or even setting fires, thereby facilitating their siege. The castle garden was built in the 1950s and is one of the earliest view architecture works in Portugal. Its designer, architect Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles, conceived this garden precisely when the castle completely ceased its military use, aiming to complement the historic site while providing visitors with a highly comfortable leisure area.

### Measure Lisbon's Old Town on Foot

Lisbon's Old Town mainly consists of four historic districts: Baixa, Chiado, Bairro Alto, and Alfama. It is recommended to split the itinerary into morning and afternoon sessions, taking about 6-7 hours in total. --- 🗺️ Classic Route Overview Morning: Baixa + Chiado Gentle terrain, perfect for starting a day of strolling 1. Rossio Square (Praça do Rossio) The central square of Lisbon, featuring distinctive black and white wave-patterned pavement. The National Theatre (Teatro Nacional D. Maria II) is located here, and in the alleys to the north, you'll find the famous Ginjinha bars, serving a traditional cherry liqueur loved by locals. 2. Santa Justa Lift (Elevador de Santa Justa) A neo-Gothic iron elevator just a 3-minute walk away, built by a student of the Eiffel Tower's designer. If the queue is short (usually 20-30 minutes), you can ride to the top for a panoramic city view; if the line is too long, it's recommended to just take photos from outside. 3. Carmo Square (Largo do Carmo) and Carmo Convent (Convento do Carmo) Gothic ruins preserved after the 1755 earthquake, with the roof collapsed and never restored, making it one of Lisbon's most striking historical sites. The convent houses an archaeological museum. 4. Chiado Square (Chiado) Known as Lisbon's "cultural heart," filled with elegant cafés, bookstores, and theaters. The famous poet Fernando Pessoa was a regular at the Brasileira café located here. 5. Camões Square (Praça Luís de Camões) At the border of Chiado and Bairro Alto, named after the author of "The Lusiads," it is a popular gathering spot for young people. Nearby are two beautiful churches: Igreja do Loreto and the Church of Our Lady of the Incarnation. --- Afternoon: Alfama Hilly terrain with maze-like medieval streets Transportation tip: From Chiado, it is recommended to take a taxi or Uber to the starting point of Alfama at Lisbon Cathedral (Sé de Lisboa) to save energy. 6. Lisbon Cathedral (Sé de Lisboa) A Romanesque cathedral built in 1147, the oldest church in Lisbon, standing firm despite multiple earthquakes. 7. Get Lost in Alfama's Alleys Key experience: turn off your navigation and wander freely! Alfama's charm lies in its maze-like narrow streets, hanging laundry, tiled walls, and sudden scenic corners. Recommended wandering time is about 1 hour. 8. Santa Luzia Viewpoint (Miradouro de Santa Luzia) Lisbon's most beautiful viewpoint, decorated with blue Azulejos tiles depicting scenes from the Reconquista, offering views over red rooftops and the Tagus River. 9. Portas do Sol Viewpoint (Miradouro das Portas do Sol) Adjacent to Santa Luzia, with a wider view, it is the best spot to capture panoramic photos of Alfama. 10. National Pantheon (Panteão Nacional) Originally the Church of Santa Engrácia, now the burial place of famous Portuguese figures. On Tuesdays and Saturdays, the nearby square hosts the Feira da Ladra flea market. 11. Monastery of São Vicente de Fora (Mosteiro de São Vicente de Fora) The burial site of the Portuguese Braganza royal family, featuring exquisite tile decorations inside. The rooftop terrace offers views of the Pantheon and the river. Admission is about €8. 12. São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) The highest point in Alfama, a Moorish castle ruin. It is recommended to allocate 1.5-2 hours to walk the walls, visit the Camera Obscura, and explore the gardens. Admission is €17, and it is advisable to buy tickets online in advance. · -- 🍽️ Food Recommendations Recommended spots and experiences: Ginjinha bars around Rossio Square Coffee and egg tarts at Brasileira café in Chiado Traditional Fado restaurants in Alfama (such as Clube de Fado) paired with Vinho Verde and codfish cakes Casa do Leão restaurant inside São Jorge Castle, where you can dine while enjoying panoramic views · -- 🚃 Transportation Tips · Tram 28: Runs through Alfama but is very crowded with tourists and often requires waiting in line. Recommended as an experience rather than main transport. · Walking: The Old Town is best explored on foot, but Alfama has many steep slopes and cobblestones, so wear comfortable, non-slip shoes. · Elevators: Besides Santa Justa, there is also the Glória Elevator (Elevador da Glória) connecting Restauradores and Bairro Alto. · -- 💡 Practical Tips Best times: · Start at 9:00 AM to avoid crowds · Visit Alfama after 3:00 PM when the light is good for photos; watch the sunset at the castle in the evening Money-saving tips: · Purchase the Lisboa Card for free public transport and access to over 51 attractions including São Jorge Castle · Many viewpoints and churches are free; you can also access the top of Santa Justa Lift for free by walking up from behind (via Carmo Convent) Safety tips: · Alfama's alleys are safe but steep and slippery; watch your step · Bring plenty of water and sunscreen in summer; dress warmly and protect against wind in winter This route covers Lisbon's complete historical timeline from Roman times, through the Moorish era, to the Pombaline reconstruction, while experiencing the most authentic neighborhood atmosphere. ### A Weekend in Lisbon: Vintage Trams, Steep Hills, and Great Food (My Experience)

I'm not usually much of a traveler. I prefer a quiet weekend at home in Amsterdam reading, gardening, or cooking up a storm. But I recently spent a few days in Lisbon. It's a beautiful, vibrant city, though quite a workout for a Dutchie accustomed to flat roads, given all the uphill and downhill walking. I had gorgeous weather—sunny with a gentle breeze—and decided to explore the city at a leisurely pace, both on foot and by tram. Here’s a look at my day, along with a few practical tips: · *Morning: Plazas and the Elevator** I kicked off my walk in the city center. The famous Santa Justa Lift was on my itinerary—a striking iron structure—but unfortunately, it was out of service when I visited. No big deal, though; the surrounding streets, paved with typical black-and-white mosaic cobblestones, are stunning to stroll through (just be careful, as they can get slippery). I wandered through the city via Rossio Square and Praça dos Restauradores. It was already quite bustling with tourists, but the vibe was incredibly laid-back. You can spot those iconic yellow trams trundling by everywhere. · *Heading to the Sé Cathedral** To save my legs a bit, I hopped on Tram 28 toward the Lisbon Cathedral (Sé). The tram was pretty packed, so definitely keep a close eye on your belongings. The cathedral itself dates back to the Middle Ages and survived massive earthquakes; it has a very solid, austere feel to it. A quick tip: pay the few extra euros to go up to the second floor. It's worth it not just for the view overlooking the nave, but especially for the way the sunlight streams through the beautiful stained-glass windows. There’s also a worthwhile little exhibition featuring ancient vestments and treasures. · *Scenic Views and the Castle** From the cathedral, it’s about a ten-minute uphill walk to the Miradouro de Santa Luzia. From this viewpoint, you can gaze out over the historic Alfama district with its sea of terracotta roofs and the Tagus River in the background. Right next door is the Castelo de São Jorge. The admission ticket includes entry to a small archaeological museum on the grounds, which I found fascinating as a history buff. The castle walls offer a sweeping, 360-degree panoramic view of the entire city. · *Evening and Dining** As evening approached, I took a leisurely stroll down toward the Rua Augusta shopping street. The sunset lighting here is absolutely magical; it bathes the colorful building facades in a warm, soft glow. I grabbed a seat at an outdoor terrace overlooking the triumphal arch. As an avid home cook, I’m always particular about food. The local 'Arroz de Marisco' (seafood rice) was incredibly flavorful and generously portioned. Naturally, I capped off the meal with a Pastel de Nata—wonderfully flaky and not overly sweet. Lisbon is an enchanting city packed with character, though you do need to be prepared for the crowds and the constant climbing. If you're planning a trip soon and have any practical questions about routes or public transit, feel free to ask!  TaleWeaver __

São Jorge CastleIt is one of the ancient buildings in Lisbon and a major historical monument and tourist attraction in Lisbon. The castle is built onAlfamaThe high point of the area was a fortress when the Moors occupied Lisbon in the Middle Ages. Located on a commanding hillside, its presence can be seen from almost every corner of Lisbon. The castle originally belonged to the earlier Visigoths. After the Moorish invasion, it underwent large-scale expansion, and its walls, up to 8 m thick, still impress with their grandeur today. Here, people can better appreciate the city's architectural art, whether fromAlfamaTo the futuristic castles and drawbridges in the distant city, or in the urbanCarmo churchThe open-air ruins can be seen at a glance. National monument The architectural complex known as Lisbon castle and Lisbon city walls was classified as a national monument under the decree issued on June 16, 1910. The monument is owned by the Portuguese state and was temporarily transferred to Lisbon city hall on September 13, 1934, with the complete transfer finalized on May 31, 1942. On June 8, 1979, the revised terms of transfer for São Jorge Castle were officially enacted. Following the resolution of the Lisbon municipal council in October 1995, São Jorge Castle was placed under the management of the municipal company Empresa de Bairros Históricos de Lisboa (EBAHL). In 2003, this management responsibility was transferred to the municipal company Empresa de Gestão de Equipamentos e Animação Cultural (EGEAC). The site consists of a castle, the ruins of the Alcázar palace, the Plaza de Armas, a spacious viewing platform overlooking the entire city, a museum exhibition area, an archaeological exhibition area, several garden areas, and the city walls. The monument covers an area of approx. 4 hectares, surrounded by a massive perimeter wall and city walls, with one section of the wall coinciding with part of the boundary of Lisbon's old castle. Space and view In the past, there were no trees inside or outside the city walls; even if there were, the quantity was far less than today. In the days when the castle was merely a fortress to be conquered, it was absolutely unacceptable to provide the enemy with any tools for climbing or even setting fires, thereby facilitating their siege. The castle garden was built in the 1950s and is one of the earliest view architecture works in Portugal. Its designer, architect Gonçalo Ribeiro Telles, conceived this garden precisely when the castle completely ceased its military use, aiming to complement the historic site while providing visitors with a highly comfortable leisure area.

### Arco da Rua Augusta Lisbon

I lived in Lisbon for 8 years and never climbed this iconic arch. Biggest mistake of my life. Honestly, I have no excuse. I walked under the Arco da Rua Augusta more times than I can count, always in a rush, always thinking "I'll do it another time." Eight years living in Lisbon. ### Portugal 12-Day Grand Tour

Portugal, a country located at the westernmost edge of Europe, tells its story through the glory of the Age of Exploration, the melancholic Fado music, the rich flavors of Port wine, and countless beautiful beaches facing the Atlantic Ocean. With abundant sunshine, friendly locals, moderate costs, and a wealth of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, Portugal is a destination that offers it all. A 12-day journey is enough to traverse the country from north to south, experiencing its diverse charm, from profound history to relaxing coastal vibes. This is not just a trip but an immersive experience that transcends time and awakens all your senses. Reasons to Visit Rich History and Heritage: As a former maritime empire, Portugal boasts numerous UNESCO World Heritage Sites. From the historic center of Porto to the Belém Tower in Lisbon and the dreamy palaces of Sintra, every step echoes with history. Unmatched Value for Money: Compared to other Western European countries, Portugal offers more affordable dining, accommodation, and transportation. You can enjoy high-quality wine, fresh seafood, and comfortable hotels on a smaller budget. Incredible Diversity: In a short trip, you can savor the rich wines of the north, the vibrant energy of Lisbon, the dramatic cliffs of Cabo da Roca at the westernmost point of Europe, and the stunning beaches and caves along the Algarve coast in the south. A Paradise for Food and Wine Lovers: Indulge in authentic Portuguese egg tarts, charcoal-grilled codfish, Port wine, and Vinho Verde. Food is the most direct and delicious way to understand Portuguese culture. Pleasant Climate and Safe Environment: With over 300 days of sunshine annually, Portugal is an ideal vacation destination. It is also one of the safest countries in Europe, making it perfect for independent travelers. Recommended Itinerary: Classic North-to-South or South-to-North Route This route efficiently connects Portugal's classic mainland destinations with a balanced pace. Day 1-3: Porto - The Fragrant Jewel of the North Activities: Stroll along the Douro River, admire the magnificent Dom Luís I Bridge, visit a Port wine cellar to learn about wine tasting, wander through the colorful Ribeira historic district, climb the Clérigos Tower for a panoramic view of the red-roofed city, and try the famous "Francesinha" sandwich. Day 4-5: Sintra + Cabo da Roca - Fairy Tales and the Edge of the World Activities: (Day 4) Take a day trip from Lisbon to explore the fairytale-like Pena Palace and the mysterious Quinta da Regaleira. (Day 5) Head to Cabo da Roca, the "end of the land and the beginning of the sea," and feel the Atlantic breeze at Europe's westernmost point. In the afternoon, visit the charming coastal town of Cascais. Day 6-8: Lisbon - The Retro and Vibrant City of Seven Hills Activities: Ride the historic Tram 28 through the Alfama district, taste the most authentic egg tarts in Belém, visit the Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower, watch the sunset under the Arco da Rua Augusta, enjoy a Fado performance, and take in panoramic views of the city from the Santa Justa Lift. Day 9-11: Algarve (Lagos/Faro) - A Feast of Sun and Coastline Activities: Relax by the seaside, take a boat or sailing tour to visit the famous Benagil Sea Cave, sunbathe and swim on stunning cliffs and golden beaches like Praia da Marinha, stroll through the old town of Lagos, and savor the freshest grilled fish. Day 12: Faro → Lisbon, Departure Activities: Spend the morning exploring Faro's old town before taking a train or driving back to Lisbon to prepare for your journey home. Transportation Tips: The best way to travel between cities is by train (CP company), which is comfortable and punctual. The Lisbon-Porto route is served by high-speed trains (Alfa Pendular). For Sintra and Cascais, consider purchasing a one-day transportation card. In the Algarve region, where attractions are spread out, renting a car offers the best experience and freedom. Photography Guide Porto: Best Spots: The south bank of the Douro River, capturing the Dom Luís I Bridge and Ribeira's colorful buildings; the viewing platform in front of the Gaia wine cellars for sunset and night views. Highlights: Snap a tram passing through the old town streets; photograph the magical staircase inside Livraria Lello (reservation/ticket required). Lisbon: Best Spots: The top of São Jorge Castle for views of the red rooftops and the Tagus River; the rooftop of the Arco da Rua Augusta; the Miradouro da Senhora do Monte viewpoint for sunsets and night views. Highlights: Capture the iconic yellow Tram 28, especially on the steep curves of the Alfama district; reflections by the water at the Belém Tower. Sintra: Best Spots: The platform in front of Pena Palace for photos of the colorful palace; looking up from the bottom of the Initiation Well at Quinta da Regaleira for a visually striking shot. Cabo da Roca: Best Spots: Pose with the cross monument, with dramatic cliffs and the endless Atlantic Ocean as the backdrop. Beware of strong winds! Algarve: Best Spots: Inside the Benagil Sea Cave, where sunlight streams through the skylight, creating a sacred and spectacular scene (accessible by boat or kayak); the cliff trail above Praia da Marinha for postcard-perfect views of the bay. Drone photography works best here. Travel Tips Best Travel Time: Spring (April-June) and Fall (September-October). The weather is sunny and warm, with fewer tourists for the best experience. July-August is peak season, very hot and crowded. Budget Planning (per person, excluding international flights): Budget Option: €600-800 (hostels, basic dining, mainly public transportation). Comfort Option: €1000-1500 (3-4 star hotels, specialty restaurants, local activities, intercity trains). Language: Portuguese. However, English is widely spoken in hotels, restaurants, and tourist attractions in major cities. Learning a few simple Portuguese phrases (e.g., Olá for hello, Obrigado/a for thank you) will make locals even happier. Must-Try Foods: Porto: Francesinha (wet sandwich), Port wine. Lisbon: Pastéis de Belém (Portuguese egg tarts), Bacalhau à Brás (charcoal-grilled codfish), Ginja (cherry liqueur). Nationwide: Grilled sardines, seafood rice (soupier than Spanish paella), Vinho Verde (green wine). Accommodation Recommendations: Porto: Ribeira district (great views but noisy), city center (convenient transportation). Lisbon: Baixa/Chiado (shopping hub), Alfama (historic charm but steep streets), Príncipe Real (trendy and quiet). Safety Tips: Portugal is generally safe, but watch out for pickpockets near popular attractions like the metro, Tram 28, and Belém Tower. Keep an eye on your belongings. Sample Budget for a Comfortable Trip: International Flights: Round-trip RMB 5000-8000 (depending on booking time and season). Accommodation: €60-120 per night for a double room, totaling €720-1440 for 12 nights (per person, half the cost). Dining: €30-50 per day for meals and snacks. Transportation: Intercity trains, local transport, and possible car rental, totaling €200-300. Tickets and Activities: Wine cellar tours, palace tickets, Fado performances, boat trips, etc., totaling €150-200. Total: A comfortable independent trip costs around €1500-2500 per person (excluding international flights). Wishing you an unforgettable journey in Portugal! Boa Viagem!

#### Best Times to Visit

*   As early as possible (10:00, opening time) – There are fewer crowds earlier in the morning, allowing a more solitary exploration experience. The weather is also cool and crisp. Sometimes there’s even a magical-feeling morning fog drifting around the estate, especially during wetter winter or spring months.
